questions.title: Groups as the unit of access management
questions.summary: Bind roles to a group once; manage churn through membership, not policy edits.
questions.question: Your company has three development teams that each need the same set of permissions on a shared development project. Team membership changes frequently as engineers join and leave. You want to minimise the ongoing administrative effort of managing access. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the required roles to each engineer's user account individually, updating bindings as people join and leave.
options.B: Create a Google group for the developers, grant the required roles to the group, and manage access by changing group membership.
options.C: Create a service account, grant it the required roles, and share its key file with the engineers.
options.D: Grant the required roles to the project's default service account and have engineers impersonate it.

explanation.summary: Groups are the unit of access management in Google Cloud IAM. Binding roles once to a group and then adding or removing members changes effective access without ever touching the IAM policy again, which keeps administrative effort flat as teams churn.

option_breakdown.A: Per-user bindings mean an IAM policy edit for every joiner and leaver, and stale bindings accumulate — the exact overhead the requirement asks you to avoid.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Roles are bound once to the group; membership becomes the only ongoing task and can be delegated or automated from your identity provider.
option_breakdown.C: Service account keys are long-lived credentials that must never be shared between humans; they are unattributable in audit logs and a serious exfiltration risk.
option_breakdown.D: Default service accounts are for workloads, not people, and letting all developers impersonate one destroys per-user attribution in audit logs.

questions.title: One view of cost across several billing accounts
questions.summary: Exporting every billing account to one BigQuery dataset gives a single queryable view across accounts.
questions.question: Resources are spread across many projects linked to different billing accounts. You need a single visual representation of all costs incurred, including new cost data as soon as it is available. What should you do?

options.A: Open the billing reports page of each billing account in turn.
options.B: Create a budget on each billing account with email notifications.
options.C: Label all resources and use the cost table report of one billing account.
options.D: Export every billing account's cost data to one BigQuery dataset and build a Looker Studio dashboard on it.

explanation.summary: Billing export can send each billing account's data to the same dataset; a dashboard on it shows all costs together and refreshes as new export data lands.

option_breakdown.A: Console reports are per billing account, so there is no single view across accounts.
option_breakdown.B: Budgets notify on thresholds; they are not a visual representation of all costs.
option_breakdown.C: A billing account's reports show only that account's projects, whatever labels exist.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Billing export can send each billing account's data to the same dataset; a dashboard on it shows all costs together and refreshes as new export data lands.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud billing accounts list  # then enable BigQuery export for each account into one dataset

questions.title: One dashboard across many projects
questions.summary: A metrics scope in one project can include other projects, giving one consolidated view.
questions.question: You need to monitor resources distributed over several Google Cloud projects and want to consolidate reporting under a single Cloud Monitoring dashboard. What should you do?

options.A: Configure a metrics scope in one project and add the other projects to it.
options.B: View each project's dashboards separately in its own Cloud Monitoring page.
options.C: Create aggregated log sinks routing every project's logs into one central log bucket.
options.D: Install the Ops Agent on the virtual machines.

explanation.summary: A metrics scope lets one scoping project observe metrics from several monitored projects, which is how Cloud Monitoring consolidates reporting for a multi-project estate into a single dashboard.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A metrics scope lets one scoping project observe metrics from several monitored projects, which is how Cloud Monitoring consolidates reporting for a multi-project estate into a single dashboard.
option_breakdown.B: Per-project views are the default and are exactly what a consolidation requirement asks you to replace.
option_breakdown.C: Aggregated sinks centralise logs; they do not consolidate metrics dashboards.
option_breakdown.D: The Ops Agent collects guest-level metrics and logs from VMs; it does not consolidate anything across projects.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud beta monitoring metrics-scopes create projects/MONITORED_PROJECT_ID \
  --project=SCOPING_PROJECT_ID

questions.title: One gcloud property to stop repeating --zone
questions.summary: Setting compute/zone as a default property on the active gcloud configuration means every subsequent command uses it automatically, without needing multiple named configurations.
questions.question: You authenticated the gcloud CLI, and most of your Compute Engine instances run in the europe-west1-d zone. You want to avoid specifying that zone on every command. What should you do?

options.C: Set europe-west1-d as the default zone using gcloud config set compute/zone
options.D: Create a separate named gcloud configuration for every zone you might ever use
options.A: Write a shell alias that appends --zone=europe-west1-d to every gcloud invocation
options.B: Rename your project so its ID embeds the zone, letting gcloud infer it automatically

explanation.summary: compute/zone is a gcloud configuration property; once set, every command that needs a zone and doesn't receive an explicit --zone flag falls back to this default, which is the direct, single-command fix for the stated annoyance.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. One property, set once, and every future command in this configuration picks up the zone automatically.
option_breakdown.D: Multiple named configurations solve a different problem — switching between several distinct environments — and are unnecessary overhead just to set one default value.
option_breakdown.A: A shell alias is a fragile, per-shell, per-machine workaround that gcloud's own configuration mechanism makes unnecessary.
option_breakdown.B: gcloud never infers a zone from a project's name or ID — this is not a real mechanism.

questions.title: Consolidate two organizations' spend onto one invoice immediately
questions.summary: A billing account is independent of the resource hierarchy it serves, so linking an acquired company's projects to your existing billing account consolidates costs right away with no organizational merge required.
questions.question: Your company has an existing Google Cloud organization with hundreds of projects on one billing account. You just acquired another company that also has hundreds of projects and its own billing account. You want to consolidate all costs onto a single invoice starting tomorrow. What should you do?

options.C: Link the acquired company's projects to your company's existing billing account
options.D: Merge the acquired company's Google Cloud organization into your own before changing any billing configuration
options.A: Wait for both billing accounts' current invoice periods to close, then manually reconcile the two invoices
options.B: Create a brand-new billing account and migrate every project from both organizations onto it

explanation.summary: A billing account and a resource-hierarchy organization are independent constructs — a project's spend is billed wherever it's linked, regardless of which organization owns the project, so simply relinking the acquired projects consolidates the invoice immediately.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This achieves same-invoice consolidation 'as of tomorrow' with no dependency on any organizational restructuring.
option_breakdown.D: Organization mergers are a much larger, slower undertaking (and not something Google Cloud performs as a simple self-service operation) that isn't actually required just to share one invoice.
option_breakdown.A: Manually reconciling two separate invoices after the fact is not the same as a single consolidated invoice, and doesn't meet the 'as of tomorrow' timeline either.
option_breakdown.B: Creating a third billing account and migrating everything is far more churn than simply relinking one company's projects to the billing account that already exists.

questions.title: Diagnose an app deployed to the wrong project via gcloud config
questions.summary: gcloud config list shows which project and account the active configuration used, which is why a deploy landed in the wrong project.
questions.question: You ran gcloud run deploy, but the service was created in the wrong project. You want to find out why, and in which project it actually landed. What should you do?

options.C: Run gcloud config list to see which project was active in your Cloud Shell session at the time of the deploy
options.D: Open the Cloud Run page in every project in your organization one at a time until you find it
options.A: Re-run gcloud run deploy with a different account and see if the result changes
options.B: File a support ticket asking Google to identify which project the deploy targeted

explanation.summary: gcloud config list shows which project and account the active configuration used, which is why a deploy landed in the wrong project.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This directly answers both 'why' (the active project wasn't what you assumed) and 'where' (the project shown in the output) in one command.
option_breakdown.D: Checking project by project is slow and does not explain why; the active configuration answers both.
option_breakdown.A: Changing the account does not reveal which project the earlier command used, and may deploy yet again.
option_breakdown.B: This information is available locally in seconds — there's no need to wait on a support ticket for something gcloud config list already tells you.

questions.title: A new project as a hard network boundary between environments
questions.summary: Separate Google Cloud projects get separate VPC networks with no connectivity between them by default, so a new project is a network isolation boundary as well as an IAM one.
questions.question: You have a development environment using Compute Engine and Cloud SQL in one project. You need to create a production environment for the same application, and the security team requires that no network routes exist between the two environments. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.C: Create a new project, enable the required APIs in it, and replicate the development setup there
options.D: Create a second VPC in the existing project for production, and rely on firewall rules alone to block traffic to the development VPC
options.A: Create a second subnet in the existing VPC for production workloads
options.B: Use IAM conditions on the existing project to prevent development resources from being reachable by production resources

explanation.summary: Each project gets its own set of VPC networks, which have zero connectivity to another project's VPCs unless something is explicitly configured (peering, Shared VPC) to connect them — a new project delivers 'no routes between environments' as a structural default, not a rule that has to be maintained.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. A separate project is network-isolated from the development project by default, satisfying the no-routes requirement without any ongoing firewall maintenance.
option_breakdown.D: Two VPCs in the same project are still both reachable to configure routes or peering between later, and relying purely on firewall rules to enforce isolation is a weaker, more error-prone control than the structural isolation a new project provides.
option_breakdown.A: Two subnets inside one VPC are, by design, reachable from each other over internal IP via the VPC's implicit routes — this is the opposite of no connectivity.
option_breakdown.B: IAM conditions govern who can call which API on which resource — they have no effect on network-layer routing or reachability between VMs.

questions.title: Reassign an existing project to the company's billing account
questions.summary: Changing a project's linked billing account moves future charges onto the new account without recreating the project or any of its resources.
questions.question: You experimented with Google Cloud on your own credit card and expensed the costs to your company. Your company now wants to streamline this by charging your project's costs directly to its own monthly invoice. What should you do?

options.C: Change the project's linked billing account to your company's billing account
options.D: Delete the project and recreate it under your company's billing account
options.A: Export your personal billing history to a spreadsheet and email it to finance every month
options.B: Ask your company to reimburse your credit card indefinitely rather than changing any billing configuration

explanation.summary: A project's billing account is just a pointer that can be swapped to a different billing account you have permission on — the project and every resource inside it keep running unchanged, and charges from that point forward land on the new account.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This is a direct configuration change with no rebuild required, and it's exactly what 'streamline the billing process' calls for.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting and recreating the project destroys every resource inside it — a drastic, disruptive way to accomplish what a billing-account swap does in seconds.
option_breakdown.A: Manual spreadsheet reconciliation is exactly the informal reimbursement process the company wants to move away from, not a streamlined replacement for it.
option_breakdown.B: Continuing to reimburse manually is the status quo the company explicitly wants to stop doing — it doesn't answer the question.

questions.title: Prerequisite for an Organization resource to exist
questions.summary: An Organization resource only exists for Google Workspace or Cloud Identity customers; projects created without one of those have no org node at all.
questions.question: A startup has been creating Google Cloud projects using individual employees' personal Gmail accounts for two years. They now want to enforce org-wide IAM policies and organization policy constraints from a single Organization node across every project. What is the prerequisite they are missing?

options.A: Nothing — every Google Cloud project automatically belongs to an Organization resource
options.B: They must set up Cloud Identity (or Google Workspace) for their domain; the Organization resource is created automatically from that
options.C: They must contact Google Cloud sales to have an Organization resource manually provisioned
options.D: They must migrate every project into a single folder, which creates the Organization node automatically

explanation.summary: The Organization resource is created automatically the moment a verified domain is set up under Cloud Identity or Google Workspace — it is not something every project has by default, and it cannot be manually requested or created by nesting projects in a folder. Standalone organisations (created automatically for new Free Trial sign-ups) do not help here: they are offered only to new customers, never to an existing set of projects.

option_breakdown.A: Wrong — a project created under a personal Gmail account has no Organization resource; the org node exists only for Cloud Identity or Workspace domains.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Setting up Cloud Identity (free, and independent of Gmail or Workspace apps) or Google Workspace for a verified domain is what causes Google to create the Organization resource; folders and org policy then attach to that node.
option_breakdown.C: No sales engagement is required — Cloud Identity is self-service and free to set up for a verified domain.
option_breakdown.D: Folders exist only underneath an Organization resource; you cannot create a folder before the org node exists, so this has the dependency backwards.

questions.title: Setting the active project for gcloud
questions.summary: The active project for a gcloud configuration is set with `gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID` — there is no `gcloud config init project` subcommand.
questions.question: You are setting up a new workstation for a developer and want their gcloud CLI to default to the team's project, my-project-test, for every subsequent command. What is the correct command?

options.A: gcloud config init project my-project-test
options.B: gcloud config set project --my-project-test
options.C: gcloud config set project my-project-test
options.D: gcloud projects set-default my-project-test

explanation.summary: `gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID` sets the project property on the active named configuration; every subsequent gcloud command that needs a project reads it from there. There is no `config init` subcommand that takes a project id this way, and no `projects set-default` command exists.

option_breakdown.A: 'gcloud config init' is not a valid pairing with a positional project id — 'gcloud init' runs the full interactive setup wizard instead; there is no 'config init project' subcommand.
option_breakdown.B: The project id is a positional argument here, not a flag value — passing it as --my-project-test would fail to parse.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. This is the direct, standard command for setting the active project on a gcloud configuration.
option_breakdown.D: There is no `gcloud projects set-default` command; project scoping for the CLI always goes through `gcloud config set project`.

questions.title: Which Compute Engine resources are global, not zonal or regional
questions.summary: Images and snapshots are global resources usable by any instance or disk in the project with no replication step; disks and instances themselves are always zonal or regional.
questions.question: A colleague is unsure which Compute Engine resource types can be referenced from any zone or region in a project without any replication step. Which pair of resources are global?

options.A: Persistent disks and instances
options.B: Images and snapshots
options.C: Static external IP addresses and subnets
options.D: Instance templates and managed instance groups

explanation.summary: Images and snapshots carry no zone or region scope: any instance or disk creation anywhere in the project can reference them directly. Disks and instances are always zonal (or regional for some disk types); static IPs and subnets are regional; and while instance templates are themselves global, managed instance groups are zonal or regional, so that pairing is mixed. (Snapshots can optionally be created as regional resources when data must stay in one region; the default standard snapshot is global.)

option_breakdown.A: Wrong — persistent disks and instances are zonal (or regional), not global; they must be created in a specific location.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Neither images nor snapshots have a zone or region scope.
option_breakdown.C: Wrong — static external IP addresses and subnets are both regional resources.
option_breakdown.D: A trap: instance templates are indeed global, but managed instance groups are zonal or regional, so this pair is not uniformly global.

questions.title: Billing must be enabled before console provisioning
questions.summary: A brand-new Google Cloud project can be created and browsed immediately, but provisioning billable resources like a VM is blocked until a billing account is linked to it.
questions.question: You're setting up Google Cloud for the first time to run a workload on Compute Engine. Which one-time step must you complete before the console will let you provision billable resources like a VM?

options.A: Specify a default compute zone for the project
options.B: Create at least one Cloud Storage bucket
options.C: Enable two-factor authentication on your account
options.D: Link the project to a billing account

explanation.summary: A project with no linked billing account can be created and browsed, but any billable resource — VMs, storage beyond the always-free tier, and so on — is blocked until billing is enabled.

option_breakdown.A: A default zone is a convenience gcloud/console property you can set (or change) anytime; it isn't required before provisioning.
option_breakdown.B: A storage bucket is itself a billable resource you can't create until billing is set up — not a prerequisite step.
option_breakdown.C: 2FA is a strong recommendation for securing your identity, not a Google Cloud provisioning requirement.
option_breakdown.D: Correct — a billing account must be linked before the project can provision billable resources.

questions.title: Chargeback across dozens of VMs by department
questions.summary: Tagging every VM with a label identifying its owning application or department is what makes per-department chargeback possible — the label flows through into billing data, letting spend be grouped and reported per label.
questions.question: Your team runs dozens of Compute Engine VMs behind three applications — two owned by marketing and one by finance. Your manager wants a way to bill each department for the VMs supporting their application. What should you put in place to make this possible?

options.A: IAM access controls restricting who can start or stop each VM
options.B: A persistent disk snapshot schedule for each application's VMs
options.C: Labels identifying the owning application or department on every VM, so spend can be grouped and reported per label
options.D: A free-text description field on each VM, filled in manually

explanation.summary: Labels are structured key/value metadata that Google Cloud billing data carries through to the detailed billing export, letting you group and report cost by label — exactly what a chargeback model needs.

option_breakdown.A: Access controls determine who can act on a VM; they carry no cost-attribution information at all.
option_breakdown.B: Snapshot schedules are a backup practice, unrelated to attributing spend to a department.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Labels flow through into billing data (including the BigQuery billing export), enabling exactly this kind of grouped reporting.
option_breakdown.D: A free-text description is for humans reading the console; billing data doesn't index or group by description text the way it does by label.

questions.title: A machine type missing from the console's create-VM list
questions.summary: The machine types Cloud Console offers when creating a VM are scoped to the selected zone — a type simply not available in that zone won't appear, regardless of subnet, OS choice, or memory settings.
questions.question: An architect recommends a specific machine type for your workload. While creating the VM in the console, that machine type doesn't appear in the list of available types. What's the most likely explanation?

options.A: You have selected the incorrect subnet
options.B: That machine type is not available in the zone you have selected
options.C: You have chosen an incompatible operating system
options.D: You have not specified a correct memory configuration

explanation.summary: Machine type availability varies by zone — not every type or CPU platform is offered everywhere. Changing the zone (or region) is the fix.

option_breakdown.A: Subnet choice affects networking, not which machine types are physically available in a zone.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. This is exactly the reason a machine type can be missing from the list.
option_breakdown.C: Machine types are compute/memory shapes, independent of the guest OS image you plan to boot.
option_breakdown.D: For a predefined machine type, memory is fixed by the type itself, not something you configure separately.

questions.title: Installing kubectl through the gcloud SDK
questions.summary: The Cloud SDK ships kubectl as an optional component installed via `gcloud components install kubectl`, not bundled by default.
questions.question: You have just installed the Google Cloud CLI on a new workstation and now want to manage Google Kubernetes Engine clusters with kubectl. The command is not yet available. What should you run to install it?

options.A: gcloud components install kubectl
options.B: gcloud components install kubernetes
options.C: gcloud components install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin
options.D: gcloud sdk install kubectl

explanation.summary: kubectl ships as an optional Cloud SDK component, installed with `gcloud components install kubectl`. A separate `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin` component is also required for GKE 1.26+ clusters using the modern authentication flow, but it is an additional component, not a substitute for kubectl itself.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the exact gcloud syntax for installing the kubectl component from the Cloud SDK's component manager.
option_breakdown.B: 'kubernetes' is not a valid component id — the component manager knows this component by the binary name, kubectl.
option_breakdown.C: gke-gcloud-auth-plugin is a real, separately installed component required for GKE authentication on modern clusters, but it does not install kubectl itself — both are needed together, not interchangeably.
option_breakdown.D: gcloud has no 'sdk install' subcommand; component management always goes through 'gcloud components install'.

questions.title: What actually drives a Compute Engine VM's price
questions.summary: VM cost is billed in per-second increments driven by the vCPU and memory of the chosen machine type, with custom machine types, Spot pricing, sustained-use discounts, and committed-use discounts all able to lower it further — there is no minimum-hour billing floor.
questions.question: You're comparing cloud providers for management and need to summarize how Compute Engine VM costs actually work. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: Every VM is force-shut-down after a maximum of 24 hours regardless of type
options.B: Sustained-use discounts are only available in a handful of regions, so cost predictability varies by location
options.C: VMs are charged for a minimum of one full hour of use no matter how briefly they actually run
options.D: VMs are billed in per-second increments, cost scales with the vCPU and memory of the chosen machine type, custom machine types are supported, Spot VMs cost dramatically less than on-demand, and further discounts apply for sustained or committed use

explanation.summary: Compute Engine bills in per-second increments (with only a short one-minute minimum), cost tracks the machine type's vCPU/memory, custom machine types exist, Spot VMs are steeply discounted, and sustained-use plus committed-use discounts stack on top.

option_breakdown.A: The 24-hour forced shutdown applied only to the legacy preemptible VM type — it is not true of on-demand, committed-use, or current Spot VMs, which can run indefinitely until reclaimed.
option_breakdown.B: Sustained-use discounts apply automatically to eligible machine-type usage regardless of region — they are not region-restricted.
option_breakdown.C: There is no one-hour billing minimum; Compute Engine moved to per-second billing (with a one-minute minimum charge) back in 2017.
option_breakdown.D: Correct on every point — per-second billing, machine-type-driven cost, custom machine types, steep Spot discounts, and sustained-use/committed-use discounts as further levers.

questions.title: Event-driven container on object finalise
questions.summary: Eventarc delivers Cloud Storage events to Cloud Run with no polling loop.
questions.question: You need to run a containerised image-processing service every time a new object is written to a Cloud Storage bucket. The service is packaged as a container, and processing must start without any polling. You want a fully managed solution with the least operational overhead. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy the container to Cloud Run and create an Eventarc trigger for the Cloud Storage object finalise event that targets the service.
options.B: Deploy the container to a managed instance group and run a cron job that lists the bucket every minute.
options.C: Deploy the container to GKE and configure a Cloud Scheduler job to invoke it every five minutes.
options.D: Configure the bucket to write object names to a Cloud SQL table and have the container poll the table.

explanation.summary: Eventarc delivers Cloud Storage events to Cloud Run natively, so the service is invoked on object finalise with no polling loop and no infrastructure to run. Cloud Run scales to zero between events.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. An Eventarc trigger on google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized pushes each new object to the Cloud Run service as it is written.
option_breakdown.B: A managed instance group with a cron job is polling by another name: it adds VMs to patch and pay for, and introduces up to a minute of latency.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Scheduler fires on a clock, not on object writes, so it misses the event-driven requirement and leaves a GKE cluster to operate.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Storage cannot write directly into Cloud SQL, and the pattern substitutes a polling loop and a database for managed event delivery.

questions.title: Minimise repeated IaC across environments
questions.summary: Terraform modules factor a repeated resource pattern into one reusable definition.
questions.question: Your company wants to standardise creation and management of many similar Google Cloud resources with Infrastructure as Code, minimising the amount of repetitive code needed to manage the environment. What should you do?

options.A: Terraform modules for each resource pattern, instantiated per environment with different variables.
options.B: A gcloud script copied per environment and edited by hand.
options.C: Export each environment's resources from the console and re-import them.
options.D: Deployment Manager templates, one per environment.

explanation.summary: A console export is a one-time snapshot, not a maintained definition.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A module defines the pattern once; each environment calls it with its own variables, which removes repeated code while keeping one reviewed definition.
option_breakdown.B: Copied scripts duplicate code and drift; they are also imperative rather than declarative.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A console export is a one-time snapshot, not a maintained definition.
option_breakdown.D: Deployment Manager is deprecated, and one template per environment is the duplication the requirement wants to remove.

questions.title: Right-sizing a managed cache instead of a DIY VM
questions.summary: A managed Memorystore instance sized to the working set beats a custom VM or a Kubernetes cluster whenever the workload is simply 'run Redis,' minimizing both operational effort and cost.
questions.question: You want to run a single caching HTTP reverse proxy for a latency-sensitive website. The proxy itself consumes almost no CPU, needs a 30-GB in-memory cache plus 2 GB of overhead, and you want to minimize cost. How should you run this?

options.C: Provision a Memorystore for Redis instance sized at 32 GB
options.D: Run it on Compute Engine using a custom instance type with 6 vCPUs and 32 GB of memory
options.A: Package it in a container and run it on GKE using n1-standard-32 nodes
options.B: Run it on Compute Engine with an n1-standard-1 instance and a 32-GB SSD persistent disk

explanation.summary: The workload's real requirement is 32 GB of managed in-memory storage with negligible compute — Memorystore bills for exactly that and removes patching, failover and cache-eviction tuning from your plate entirely.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. A right-sized managed Redis instance matches the memory requirement precisely and needs no operational overhead for a near-zero-CPU workload.
option_breakdown.D: A custom 6-vCPU VM pays for CPU capacity this workload will never use, and you still own OS patching and Redis administration yourself.
option_breakdown.A: n1-standard-32 nodes provide 32 vCPUs each — wildly oversized for a workload that 'consumes almost no CPU,' and GKE adds cluster management overhead with no benefit here.
option_breakdown.B: An SSD persistent disk is durable block storage, not in-memory cache — reads would hit disk latency instead of RAM, defeating the point of a caching proxy.

questions.title: Two subnets, two regions, no extra routes needed
questions.summary: A VPC's implicit routes cover every subnet in every region attached to it automatically, so instances in different regional subnets of the same VPC reach each other over internal IP with zero extra configuration.
questions.question: You have production and test workloads to deploy on Compute Engine. Production VMs must be in a different subnet than test VMs, and all VMs must reach each other over internal IP with no additional routes created. Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.C: Create a single custom-mode VPC with two subnets in different regions, each with its own CIDR range
options.D: Create two separate VPCs, one for production and one for test, and peer them
options.A: Create a single legacy network with one flat IP range shared by both workloads
options.B: Create a single custom-mode VPC with two subnets in the same region and same CIDR range

explanation.summary: A VPC is a global resource: every subnet you add, in any region, is automatically reachable from every other subnet in the same VPC over internal IP through implicit system routes, with no peering or manual routes required.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. One VPC with two distinct-CIDR subnets satisfies both the separation requirement and the no-extra-routes requirement — VPC-wide implicit routing handles reachability automatically.
option_breakdown.D: Two separate VPCs are not connected by default; peering is exactly the 'additional configuration' the requirement rules out, and it isn't even routes in the traditional sense but a separate mechanism.
option_breakdown.A: A flat shared range does not separate production from test into distinct subnets at all.
option_breakdown.B: Two subnets cannot share the same CIDR range within one VPC — the ranges must be non-overlapping, and same-region placement isn't actually required by the scenario.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute networks subnets create prod-subnet --network=VPC_NAME --region=us-central1 --range=10.0.1.0/24 && gcloud compute networks subnets create test-subnet --network=VPC_NAME --region=europe-west1 --range=10.0.2.0/24

questions.title: Bake in Automatic Restart and live migration for HA
questions.summary: Automatic Restart recovers a crashed VM and 'Migrate VM instance' on-host maintenance keeps it running through a live host maintenance event — both are per-instance availability settings baked into the template.
questions.question: You want to configure 10 Compute Engine instances so they attempt to automatically restart if they crash, and remain highly available through host maintenance events. What should you do?

options.C: Create an instance template with Automatic Restart set to on and On-host maintenance set to 'Migrate VM instance,' and use the template in an instance group
options.D: Create an instance template with Automatic Restart set to off and On-host maintenance set to 'Terminate,' and use the template in an instance group
options.A: Rely on the default Compute Engine SLA with no configuration changes needed
options.B: Set up a Cloud Monitoring alert that pages an on-call engineer to manually restart any crashed instance

explanation.summary: Automatic Restart and on-host maintenance behavior are exactly the two per-instance knobs Compute Engine offers for these two failure modes: a crash restarts the instance, and Migrate keeps it running by live-migrating to another host during planned maintenance instead of stopping it.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This is the direct configuration for both stated requirements — self-healing on crash, live migration through maintenance.
option_breakdown.D: This is the inverse configuration: it disables automatic restart and forces the VM to stop during maintenance, the opposite of what's required.
option_breakdown.A: Defaults do not guarantee this behavior is explicitly enabled, and the requirement calls for an explicit, verifiable configuration.
option_breakdown.B: A human-paged manual restart is slower and less reliable than the platform's built-in automatic restart, and does nothing for the maintenance-availability requirement.

questions.title: Reach Cloud Storage from on-premises with no public internet path
questions.summary: Private Google Access from on-premises routes traffic to Google APIs over your VPN or Interconnect by advertising restricted.googleapis.com's dedicated range and resolving *.googleapis.com to it, with no public IP or internet path anywhere.
questions.question: You host an application on bare-metal servers in your own data center. The application needs access to Cloud Storage, but security policy forbids those servers from having public IP addresses or internet access. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.C: Using Cloud VPN or Interconnect, build a tunnel to a VPC; advertise the restricted.googleapis.com range 199.36.153.4/30 over Cloud Router; and configure on-premises DNS to resolve *.googleapis.com as a CNAME to restricted.googleapis.com
options.D: Assign each on-premises server a public IP address, and restrict access with a firewall allow-list of Google's published IP ranges
options.A: Deploy a NAT gateway in the data center and route all Cloud Storage traffic through the public internet via NAT
options.B: Copy the required objects to a portable drive and physically transport them to the data center

explanation.summary: This is the documented hybrid pattern for reaching Google APIs privately: the VPN or Interconnect tunnel carries the traffic, the restricted VIP range is advertised into on-premises routing, and DNS resolution sends *.googleapis.com traffic to that private range instead of the public internet.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. Every piece of this — tunnel, route advertisement, DNS override — is required together to reach googleapis.com entirely over private connectivity.
option_breakdown.D: Assigning public IPs directly contradicts the stated security policy that forbids public addressing on these servers.
option_breakdown.A: Routing through NAT to the public internet is exactly the internet path the security policy prohibits, even though the servers themselves lack public IPs.
option_breakdown.B: Physical media transport is not a general-purpose, ongoing access solution — it does not scale to an application that needs interactive access to Cloud Storage.

questions.title: BigQuery external table over an AVRO file, no load step
questions.summary: A BigQuery external table queries a Cloud Storage object with plain SQL in place, giving SQL-only analysts instant access without a load job moving or duplicating the data.
questions.question: You have a large 5-TB AVRO file stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. Your analysts are proficient only in SQL and need access to the data as soon as possible, at the lowest cost. What should you do?

options.D: Create a BigQuery external table pointing at the Cloud Storage object, and let analysts run SQL queries against it directly
options.A: Load the entire 5-TB file into a native BigQuery table before allowing any queries
options.B: Export the AVRO file to CSV, then have analysts download and query it with a spreadsheet tool
options.C: Stand up a Dataproc cluster and teach analysts to write Spark SQL against the file

explanation.summary: AVRO is one of BigQuery's natively supported external formats, so an external table lets analysts query it with ordinary SQL immediately, skipping the time and storage cost of loading 5 TB into a managed table first.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. This gets SQL-only analysts querying immediately with no load job and no duplicated storage cost.
option_breakdown.A: Loading 5 TB before any query can run is slower and doubles storage cost — needless, since external tables read AVRO directly.
option_breakdown.B: A 5-TB export as CSV is impractical to download, and spreadsheet tools cannot handle data at this scale at all.
option_breakdown.C: Standing up and administering a Dataproc cluster, then having SQL-only analysts learn Spark SQL, is far more operational effort and a skills mismatch versus a BigQuery external table.

questions.title: Archive, not Coldline, for once-a-year access
questions.summary: Coldline is priced for roughly quarterly access; when the true pattern is annual or less, Archive's lower storage price wins even though its retrieval fee is higher.
questions.question: You need a solution for storing and archiving data to support compliance objectives for data from a single geographic location. The data is archived after 30 days and needs to be accessed once a year. What should you do?

options.A: Select Regional Storage, and add a lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Coldline Storage
options.B: Select Regional Storage, and add a lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Archive Storage
options.C: Select Multi-Regional Storage, and add a lifecycle rule that archives data after 30 days to Nearline Storage
options.D: Select Regional Storage, and leave the data in Standard class since 30 days is too short a window to bother archiving

explanation.summary: Coldline's pricing is calibrated around roughly quarterly retrieval (its 90-day minimum storage duration matches that cadence); an annual-or-rarer access pattern falls past that threshold, where Archive's lower per-GB storage price produces the lower total cost even after accounting for its higher per-retrieval fee.

option_breakdown.A: Coldline is the right answer for quarterly access, but for truly annual access its higher storage price (versus Archive) loses on total cost given only one retrieval a year.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A single-region compliance archive touched about once a year is exactly Archive class's target pattern — lowest storage cost, retrieval cost paid rarely.
option_breakdown.C: Multi-regional storage pays a locality premium the single-geography requirement doesn't need, and Nearline's 30-day cadence assumption doesn't match once-a-year access either.
option_breakdown.D: Leaving data in Standard class after 30 days pays the highest ongoing storage price for data that is barely ever read — the opposite of cost-effective.

questions.title: gVisor sandbox isolates arbitrary customer code per tenant
questions.summary: A GKE Sandbox node pool runs each customer's Pod inside a gVisor-isolated kernel boundary, the strongest Pod-level isolation GKE offers short of a fully separate cluster.
questions.question: You are building a product on GKE where each of your customers runs a Pod containing arbitrary code they control. You want to maximize isolation between customers' Pods. What should you do?

options.D: Create a GKE node pool with sandbox type set to gvisor, and add runtimeClassName: gvisor to each customer Pod's spec
options.A: Rely on Kubernetes Namespaces alone to separate each customer's Pod
options.B: Apply resource requests and limits to each Pod so no customer can starve another of CPU or memory
options.C: Run every customer's Pod as a distinct Kubernetes user with RBAC restricting access to their own Namespace

explanation.summary: gVisor interposes a user-space kernel between each container and the host, containing a container-escape exploit that would otherwise reach the shared node kernel — Namespaces, resource limits and RBAC all operate above that boundary and do not address it.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. GKE Sandbox is purpose-built for exactly this: strong kernel-level isolation between mutually untrusted workloads sharing a cluster.
option_breakdown.A: Namespaces are a logical partitioning of the Kubernetes API and object visibility — they provide no kernel-level isolation between containers running on the same node.
option_breakdown.B: Resource requests and limits prevent noisy-neighbor resource contention, not a security boundary against a malicious or compromised container escaping to the host.
option_breakdown.C: RBAC controls who can call the Kubernetes API and what they can do there — it says nothing about isolation between running containers on a shared kernel.

questions.title: Avoid a hot Spanner split with a non-monotonic primary key
questions.summary: A monotonically increasing primary key concentrates every insert on the same Spanner split, so choosing a key that distributes writes evenly is the fix for that specific latency pattern.
questions.question: Your Cloud Spanner application shows read-latency issues on a table that is accessed only by primary key, and the table currently uses an auto-incrementing integer as its primary key. You want to resolve the issue. What should you do?

options.D: Change the primary key so its values are not monotonically increasing, for example by using a UUID or a hashed prefix
options.A: Add a secondary index on the primary key column
options.B: Increase the number of Spanner processing units to add more compute capacity
options.C: Switch the table's primary key to a composite of every column in the table

explanation.summary: Spanner shards data by key range across splits; an ever-increasing key means every new row — and every lookup near the end of the range — lands on the same split, creating a hotspot that adding compute or an index cannot fix, since the load is concentrated by key layout, not by total capacity.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. A non-monotonic key (UUID, hash prefix, or a bit-reversed sequence) spreads rows and their access pattern evenly across splits, eliminating the hotspot.
option_breakdown.A: A secondary index still needs to be maintained and would carry the same hotspotting risk if it is also ordered by a monotonically increasing value.
option_breakdown.B: More processing units add aggregate capacity across the instance, but a single overloaded split is still bottlenecked on that one split's resources — capacity elsewhere doesn't help it.
option_breakdown.C: A key made of every column doesn't address the root cause (monotonic ordering) and would make lookups and writes far more unwieldy for no isolation benefit.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql DATABASE_ID --instance=INSTANCE_ID --sql="SELECT ... WHERE key_prefix = ..."

questions.title: Provision a long monthly batch as start/stop, not always-on
questions.summary: A workload that only needs to exist for the duration of a scheduled run is cheapest as a Compute Engine VM started before the job and stopped after, rather than an instance left running continuously.
questions.question: Your company runs one on-premises batch process that takes around 30 hours, runs monthly, can execute offline, and must be restartable if interrupted. You want to migrate it to the cloud while minimizing cost. What should you do?

options.D: Migrate the workload to a Compute Engine VM, and start and stop the instance around the monthly run
options.A: Migrate the workload to a Compute Engine VM, and leave it running continuously all month
options.B: Migrate the workload to a fleet of Cloud Run services kept warm 24/7
options.C: Migrate the workload to an always-on GKE Autopilot cluster sized for the batch job's peak resource needs

explanation.summary: Compute Engine bills by the second while an instance is running — a job that only needs ~30 hours once a month is cheapest run on a VM that is started right before the job and stopped right after, rather than paying for the other ~700 idle hours in the month.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. Starting and stopping the VM around the schedule pays for compute only while the job is actually running, matching the requirement to minimize cost.
option_breakdown.A: Leaving the VM running for the entire month pays for roughly 95% idle time when the job only needs about 30 hours out of ~720.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Run is built for request-driven, typically short-lived workloads, not a 30-hour continuous batch job, and 'kept warm 24/7' pays for idle capacity the same way option B does.
option_breakdown.C: An always-on cluster sized for peak batch load pays for that peak-sized capacity every hour of the month, the most expensive option of the four for an infrequent job.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instances start INSTANCE_NAME --zone=ZONE && gcloud compute instances stop INSTANCE_NAME --zone=ZONE

questions.title: Device-prefixed row keys for high-throughput IoT telemetry
questions.summary: A Bigtable row key built from a device identifier prefix plus timestamp spreads writes across tablets, while a timestamp-only key concentrates every device's simultaneous writes onto the single tablet serving the current time range.
questions.question: Your company rents out construction equipment fitted with sensors that emit event data every few seconds — engine status, distance, fuel level. You expect thousands of events per hour per device and need consistent, atomic retrieval by time of event. What should you do?

options.D: Ingest the data into Cloud Bigtable, using a row key composed of the device ID followed by a reverse or bucketed timestamp
options.A: Ingest the data into Cloud Bigtable, using a row key based only on the event timestamp
options.B: Ingest the data into Cloud Bigtable, using a randomly generated UUID as the row key with the timestamp stored as a column value
options.C: Ingest the data directly into BigQuery via streaming inserts, keyed by device ID

explanation.summary: A timestamp-only key sorts every device's near-simultaneous writes into the same narrow key range, hotspotting the single tablet serving that range at any moment; prefixing with device ID distributes writes across tablets by device while still keeping each device's events sorted together for efficient time-range scans.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. Device-prefixed keys spread the write load across the keyspace by device while preserving fast, ordered per-device time-range reads — exactly the throughput and retrieval pattern described.
option_breakdown.A: A pure timestamp key means all devices write to the same narrow, constantly-advancing key range simultaneously — the classic Bigtable hotspotting anti-pattern, not a fix for high throughput.
option_breakdown.B: A random UUID avoids hotspotting but destroys the ability to efficiently scan a time range for a given device, since related events are no longer stored contiguously.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery streaming inserts are built for analytical querying at scale, not for the atomic, low-latency single-row reads and writes this device-telemetry pattern calls for.

questions.title: In-memory ERP database needs a memory-optimized machine family
questions.summary: An application that holds its entire database in memory needs the memory-to-vCPU ratio of Compute Engine's memory-optimized M-series, which scales to multiple terabytes of RAM per instance.
questions.question: You are deploying a new Enterprise Resource Planning system that holds its full database in memory for fast access. You need to configure the most appropriate Compute Engine resources for this application. What should you do?

options.D: Provision Compute Engine instances from the memory-optimized machine family (M-series)
options.A: Provision Compute Engine instances from the compute-optimized machine family (C-series)
options.B: Provision Compute Engine instances from the general-purpose E2 machine family with the smallest available memory footprint
options.C: Provision Compute Engine instances from a Local SSD-only configuration with minimal RAM

explanation.summary: In-memory databases like SAP HANA are the canonical workload for the memory-optimized family, whose machine types offer a far higher memory-to-vCPU ratio — up to multiple terabytes of RAM per instance — than general-purpose or compute-optimized families provide.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. The memory-optimized family exists specifically for workloads that need to hold very large datasets entirely in RAM.
option_breakdown.A: Compute-optimized machines maximize per-core performance for CPU-bound workloads (like gaming or HPC) and do not offer the large memory footprint this workload needs.
option_breakdown.B: A general-purpose family with the smallest memory footprint is the opposite of what an in-memory-database workload requires.
option_breakdown.C: Local SSD is fast ephemeral block storage, not RAM — it does not substitute for the memory capacity an in-memory database engine needs to hold data.

questions.title: Single-instance VM restarts itself with a size-1 MIG
questions.summary: A Managed Instance Group with autoscaling fixed to a minimum and maximum of one instance behaves as a self-healing single VM: exactly one instance runs at all times, automatically recreated if it fails.
questions.question: You are deploying an application to a Compute Engine VM inside a Managed Instance Group. The application must always be running, but exactly one instance of the VM should exist per project at any time. How should you configure the instance group?

options.D: Enable autoscaling, and set both the minimum and maximum number of instances to 1
options.A: Disable autoscaling, and manually recreate the instance whenever it fails
options.B: Enable autoscaling with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 5, and monitor manually to keep it near 1
options.C: Run the VM outside of any instance group, and rely on Automatic Restart alone

explanation.summary: Pinning both bounds to 1 tells the MIG's health-checking and autohealing machinery to keep exactly one instance running at all times, automatically recreating it on failure — satisfying both 'always running' and 'exactly one instance' without any manual intervention.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. This configuration gives self-healing (via the group) while structurally guaranteeing the instance count never goes above or below one.
option_breakdown.A: Manual recreation on failure is slower than the group's automatic recreation and defeats the purpose of using a Managed Instance Group at all.
option_breakdown.B: A max of 5 permits the group to scale beyond one instance under load, violating the 'exactly one instance' requirement, and manual monitoring to hold it near 1 is an unreliable substitute for a hard limit.
option_breakdown.C: Automatic Restart alone (outside a MIG) only recovers from a host-level failure; it doesn't recreate the instance if the VM itself is deleted or its boot disk becomes unusable, which a MIG's health check and recreation logic does cover.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling MIG_NAME --zone=ZONE --min-num-replicas=1 --max-num-replicas=1

questions.title: Node auto-upgrade keeps a GKE cluster on a supported version
questions.summary: Enabling node auto-upgrade lets GKE keep a cluster's nodes on a supported, stable Kubernetes version automatically, without an operator tracking version deprecation dates by hand.
questions.question: You create a new GKE cluster and want to make sure it always runs a supported and stable version of Kubernetes without manual intervention. What should you do?

options.D: Enable node auto-upgrade for the GKE cluster's node pools
options.A: Manually check the Kubernetes release notes each quarter and upgrade nodes by hand when a version nears end of support
options.B: Pin the cluster to a fixed Kubernetes version at creation time and never change it
options.C: Disable the control plane's automatic upgrades so nodes and control plane never drift out of sync

explanation.summary: Node auto-upgrade has GKE apply new patch and minor versions to node pools on Google's schedule, keeping nodes aligned with a supported version and with the control plane's own version, with no manual tracking or intervention required.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. This directly automates staying on a supported version, matching the 'without manual intervention' requirement exactly.
option_breakdown.A: A manual quarterly check is exactly the human process the requirement asks to avoid, and it's easy to miss a deprecation window between checks.
option_breakdown.B: A version pinned forever eventually falls out of Google's supported version window entirely, the opposite of 'always runs a supported version.'
option_breakdown.C: Disabling automatic upgrades removes the very automation this requirement is asking for, and control-plane/node version skew has supported limits regardless of this setting.

questions.title: Unified batch and streaming ETL without managing servers
questions.summary: Dataflow is the managed Apache Beam runner for unified batch and streaming pipelines, autoscaling workers with no cluster to size or patch.
questions.question: Your team needs a single pipeline definition that can run the same transformation logic as either a nightly batch job or a continuous streaming job, ingesting from Pub/Sub or Cloud Storage, with Google managing worker autoscaling and no cluster to provision. Which service should you use?

options.A: Cloud Dataproc, running a Spark Structured Streaming job on a manually sized cluster
options.B: BigQuery scheduled queries, reading directly from a federated Pub/Sub source
options.C: Cloud Composer, orchestrating a DAG of Cloud Run functions for each pipeline stage
options.D: Cloud Dataflow, using the Apache Beam unified batch/streaming programming model

explanation.summary: Dataflow's core value proposition is Apache Beam's unified model, where the same pipeline code runs as batch or streaming, while Google fully manages worker provisioning and autoscaling — matching every requirement in the scenario.

option_breakdown.A: Dataproc requires you to size and manage the underlying Hadoop/Spark cluster yourself — the opposite of 'no cluster to provision'.
option_breakdown.B: BigQuery is a data warehouse; it does not run arbitrary streaming transformation pipelines against a Pub/Sub source this way.
option_breakdown.C: Composer orchestrates scheduled or dependency-based workflows; it is not itself a unified batch/stream execution engine.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Dataflow plus Apache Beam is purpose-built for exactly this unified batch/streaming, fully managed requirement.

questions.title: The three database engines Cloud SQL supports
questions.summary: Cloud SQL is a fully managed service for exactly three engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server.
questions.question: A .NET team wants to lift-and-shift an existing Microsoft SQL Server database to a fully managed Google Cloud database service without changing database engines. Is this possible with Cloud SQL?

options.A: Yes — Cloud SQL offers fully managed instances for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server
options.B: No — Cloud SQL only supports MySQL and PostgreSQL; SQL Server requires a self-managed Compute Engine instance
options.C: Yes, but only in a limited preview available by invitation
options.D: No — Microsoft SQL Server workloads must move to Cloud Spanner, which supports the T-SQL dialect

explanation.summary: Cloud SQL for SQL Server is a generally available, fully managed engine alongside MySQL and PostgreSQL, so a SQL-Server-based lift-and-shift with no engine change is a supported, mainstream path.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cloud SQL supports exactly three engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server, all fully managed and GA.
option_breakdown.B: Outdated — SQL Server support on Cloud SQL has been generally available for years, not something requiring self-management.
option_breakdown.C: Not preview-gated; Cloud SQL for SQL Server is broadly generally available.
option_breakdown.D: Spanner does not speak the T-SQL dialect — it exposes GoogleSQL and a PostgreSQL-compatible interface, neither of which is a SQL Server engine-compatibility target.

questions.title: Mounting a Cloud Storage bucket as a filesystem on a VM
questions.summary: Cloud Storage FUSE lets a Compute Engine instance mount a bucket and interact with objects through familiar filesystem semantics, distinct from Filestore's true NFS POSIX compliance.
questions.question: A legacy application on a Compute Engine VM expects to read and write flat files under a local directory path, but you want the underlying data to actually live in a Cloud Storage bucket rather than on a persistent disk. You do not need full POSIX file-locking semantics. What is the simplest way to give the application that directory-style view of bucket objects?

options.A: Provision a Filestore instance and NFS-mount it, then use `gcloud storage rsync` on a cron job to keep it synced with the bucket
options.B: Attach the bucket as a persistent disk using `gcloud compute disks create --source-bucket`
options.C: Install Cloud Storage FUSE on the VM and mount the bucket directly as a local directory
options.D: Enable Cloud CDN on the bucket so the VM can access it over a local loopback address

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage FUSE is exactly the tool for mounting a GCS bucket as a local filesystem path, giving object storage a directory-style interface for applications that expect one, without requiring true POSIX guarantees.

option_breakdown.A: Filestore plus a periodic rsync adds an unnecessary second storage tier and a sync lag — overkill and stale compared to a direct mount.
option_breakdown.B: No such flag or mechanism exists; persistent disks cannot be backed directly by a Cloud Storage bucket.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud Storage FUSE mounts a bucket as a local directory with a single install-and-mount step.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud CDN caches HTTP(S) responses at the network edge for external consumers; it has nothing to do with local filesystem mounting.

questions.title: Fast durable block storage that isn't Local SSD
questions.summary: SSD persistent disks give network-attached, zone-replicated block storage up to 64 TB per disk — durable across instance and even host failure, unlike Local SSD's ephemeral capacity.
questions.question: You need block storage for a Compute Engine VM that must survive the VM being stopped, deleted and recreated, offer consistently fast IOPS, and scale to tens of terabytes on a single volume. Cost is a secondary concern. Which disk type fits, and how large can a single volume get?

options.A: Standard persistent disk, sized for capacity rather than IOPS
options.B: Local SSD, up to several terabytes, but data is lost if the instance stops
options.C: Hyperdisk Throughput, optimized specifically for large sequential scans
options.D: SSD persistent disk, up to 64 TB, durable independent of the VM lifecycle

explanation.summary: SSD persistent disk is network-attached, durable block storage decoupled from any single VM, scaling to 64 TB per disk with strong steady IOPS — matching every stated requirement, including surviving stop, delete and recreate.

option_breakdown.A: Standard (HDD-backed) persistent disk tops out at meaningfully lower IOPS than SSD persistent disk, the wrong fit when consistently fast performance matters.
option_breakdown.B: Correctly flags Local SSD's ephemerality, which disqualifies it here — its contents do not survive the instance stopping, let alone being deleted and recreated.
option_breakdown.C: Hyperdisk Throughput is a real, powerful option, but it's tuned for high-throughput sequential access rather than general fast durable block storage — a more specialized fit than this scenario calls for.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. SSD persistent disk meets durability, IOPS and the 64 TB capacity ceiling all at once.

questions.title: Guaranteed discount for predictable steady-state VM usage
questions.summary: Committed Use Discounts trade a 1- or 3-year spend or resource commitment for a deep, guaranteed discount — the right lever when usage is steady and known in advance, unlike Spot's interruption risk or on-demand pricing's flexibility premium.
questions.question: Your analytics team runs the same fleet of Compute Engine VMs 24/7, year-round, with usage that has been flat and predictable for the past year. Finance wants the deepest possible discount on this steady-state compute spend, and the workload cannot tolerate interruption. What pricing model should you apply?

options.A: Spot VMs, which offer the largest discount of any Compute Engine pricing model
options.B: Committed Use Discounts, committing to a 1- or 3-year term in exchange for a discount on guaranteed, non-interruptible capacity
options.C: On-demand pricing with automatic sustained-use style discounting as the primary lever for the deepest possible savings
options.D: Reserved Instances, purchased through the Marketplace

explanation.summary: Committed Use Discounts are Google's mechanism for steady, predictable, non-interruptible workloads: commit to spend or a specific resource for 1 or 3 years for a deep discount, with full availability guaranteed — unlike Spot, which offers deeper discounts but with arbitrary interruption risk.

option_breakdown.A: Spot VMs give the deepest discount of any Compute Engine option, but at the cost of arbitrary interruption — disqualified by 'cannot tolerate interruption'.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. CUDs are the purpose-built lever for exactly this steady-state, interruption-intolerant, cost-sensitive scenario.
option_breakdown.C: Automatic discounting on-demand is not the tool to reach for when finance specifically wants the deepest guaranteed discount by design — CUDs are the primary lever for that.
option_breakdown.D: 'Reserved Instances' is AWS terminology and not a real Google Cloud product name or Marketplace purchase; Google's equivalent mechanism is Committed Use Discounts.

questions.title: Config drift from undocumented manual changes
questions.summary: Manual, undocumented changes to VM configuration cause drift with no audit trail; the fix is to make every change through version-controlled, repeatable automation — gcloud scripts under source control at minimum, or better, a declarative IaC tool like Terraform.
questions.question: You lead a team of cloud engineers maintaining resources for several departments. You've noticed configuration drift — some VMs no longer match how they were originally provisioned, and nobody can find notes explaining what changed or why. What practice addresses this?

options.A: Require all engineers to use only the Cloud Shell command line, never the console
options.B: Take notes on each change and store them in a shared document
options.C: Restrict change privileges to a single engineer so all changes are known to one person
options.D: Encode changes as scripts — ideally declarative IaC such as Terraform, or at minimum version-controlled gcloud scripts — and keep them in a version control system

explanation.summary: Scripted, version-controlled changes are self-documenting — the diff shows exactly what changed, and the commit message can say why — and repeatable across machines. A declarative tool like Terraform goes further, since it can detect and reconcile drift automatically by comparing declared state against reality.

option_breakdown.A: Restricting to the CLI doesn't by itself create a record of what was run or why — a human can still run untracked ad hoc commands there just as easily as in the console.
option_breakdown.B: Notes in a document rely on humans remembering to write them accurately and consistently — the exact discipline that already failed here.
option_breakdown.C: A single-engineer bottleneck doesn't scale, creates an availability risk, and still isn't a durable record — it just relocates undocumented tribal knowledge into one person's memory.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Version-controlled, scripted or declarative change management directly fixes both symptoms: the drift itself and the missing documentation of why it happened.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instances describe INSTANCE_NAME --format=yaml > instance-state.yaml

questions.title: GPUs must be compatible with the chosen machine type's CPU
questions.summary: Not every GPU model is compatible with every machine type, and GPU availability is further scoped per zone — that compatibility and zonal availability, not provisioning model, disk count, or OS version, is what determines whether a GPU can be attached.
questions.question: You're planning to attach a GPU to a new Compute Engine instance. Which constraint must you satisfy for the GPU to actually work?

options.A: The instance must be Spot/preemptible
options.B: The chosen GPU model must be compatible with the chosen machine type, and available in the target zone
options.C: The instance must have no non-boot disks attached
options.D: The instance must boot from an Ubuntu image

explanation.summary: GPU-to-machine-type compatibility and zonal availability are the real constraints to check before attaching a GPU; provisioning model, extra disks, and a specific OS version are unrelated.

option_breakdown.A: GPUs attach to on-demand, committed-use, or Spot instances alike — Spot/preemptible is not a requirement.
option_breakdown.B: Correct — GPU-to-machine-type compatibility and per-zone availability are the actual constraints.
option_breakdown.C: Non-boot (additional) disks can coexist with a GPU with no conflict.
option_breakdown.D: GPUs work on the supported Linux and Windows images once drivers are installed; the OS family is not the constraint.

questions.title: Instance groups are the building block for scaling and HA
questions.summary: Managed instance groups add and remove homogeneous instances automatically based on load and can span multiple zones; pairing one with a load balancer is what delivers both scalability and high availability for an application.
questions.question: You're deploying an application that must scale with demand and stay highly available across failures. Which Compute Engine component directly provides this?

options.A: Spot instances
options.B: Instance groups, paired with a load balancer
options.C: Cloud Storage
options.D: GPUs

explanation.summary: Managed instance groups are the scaling/HA primitive — they can autoscale and span multiple zones — and pairing one with a load balancer is exactly what delivers both scalability and availability.

option_breakdown.A: Spot instances can be reclaimed by Google at any time, which works against — not for — availability.
option_breakdown.B: Correct — instance groups (especially managed ones) plus a load balancer is the standard scaling/HA pattern.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Storage is an object storage service, unrelated to compute scaling or availability.
option_breakdown.D: GPUs accelerate specific compute-heavy workloads; they don't affect scaling or availability.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instance-groups managed create GROUP_NAME --template=TEMPLATE_NAME --size=2

questions.title: A managed instance group needs an instance template first
questions.summary: A managed instance group creates and manages its own instances automatically from an instance template — the template must exist first; you don't pre-create instances, and no standalone boot image or snapshot is a prerequisite by itself.
questions.question: Before you can create a managed instance group, what must already exist?

options.A: The individual instances that will belong to the group
options.B: An instance template defining how each instance should be created
options.C: A boot disk image, created separately from any template
options.D: A source snapshot for the group's disks

explanation.summary: The instance template is the required prerequisite for a managed instance group: it specifies machine type, image, disks, and metadata, and the group provisions instances from it automatically.

option_breakdown.A: Instances are created automatically by the managed group from the template — you don't pre-create them yourself.
option_breakdown.B: Correct — the instance template must exist first; the group provisions instances from it.
option_breakdown.C: A boot disk image is referenced from inside the template, not required as a separate standalone prerequisite.
option_breakdown.D: A source snapshot isn't required to create a managed instance group; it's only relevant if a template's disk happens to be sourced from one.

questions.title: Managed instance group autoscaling can key off several signals
questions.summary: MIG autoscaling policies can combine several signal types — average CPU utilization, a custom Cloud Monitoring metric, load balancing serving capacity, and queue-based workload signals — rather than being limited to a single fixed metric.
questions.question: What can trigger a managed instance group to scale up the number of instances it runs?

options.A: CPU utilization and operating system updates only
options.B: Disk usage and CPU utilization only
options.C: CPU utilization, a custom Cloud Monitoring metric, load balancing serving capacity, or a queue-based workload signal
options.D: Disk usage and operating system updates only

explanation.summary: MIG autoscaling policies can combine average CPU utilization, a custom Cloud Monitoring metric, HTTP(S) load balancing serving capacity, and queue-based workload signals such as Cloud Tasks queue depth — this is the documented basis for scale-up decisions.

option_breakdown.A: Operating system updates don't drive autoscaling decisions at all.
option_breakdown.B: Disk usage alone isn't one of the built-in autoscaling signal types.
option_breakdown.C: Correct — these four signal types are the documented basis for MIG autoscaling policies.
option_breakdown.D: Same issue as A/B — OS updates aren't an autoscaling signal, and disk usage isn't either.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling GROUP_NAME --max-num-replicas=10 --target-cpu-utilization=0.6

questions.title: Unmanaged instance groups fit a heterogeneous legacy cluster
questions.summary: Managed instance groups require every instance to come from one shared template, which can't represent genuinely different node configurations — unmanaged instance groups exist for exactly this narrow case: grouping pre-existing, heterogeneous instances under one load balancer.
questions.question: You're lifting a legacy load-balanced cluster into Compute Engine with minimal architectural change. Its nodes run two different configurations by design, and load is steady enough that scaling is rarely needed. Which Compute Engine resource fits this cluster best?

options.A: Spot instances
options.B: Unmanaged instance groups
options.C: Managed instance groups
options.D: GPUs

explanation.summary: Unmanaged instance groups are the recommended-if-limited-use fit when instances must keep differing configurations under one load balancer, since managed instance groups enforce a single shared template across every member.

option_breakdown.A: Spot instances address cost and reclaimability, not the heterogeneous-configuration constraint described here.
option_breakdown.B: Correct — unmanaged instance groups are built for exactly this narrow case of pre-existing, differently configured instances.
option_breakdown.C: Managed instance groups enforce a single instance template across every member, which this two-configuration cluster can't satisfy without a redesign.
option_breakdown.D: GPUs are unrelated to how the cluster's nodes are grouped or load-balanced.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instance-groups unmanaged create GROUP_NAME --zone=ZONE

questions.title: Validate IaC dependencies before committing
questions.summary: A dry-run plan resolves the dependency graph without creating anything.
questions.question: You have significantly changed a complex infrastructure-as-code configuration and want to confirm that the dependencies between all defined resources are properly met before committing the change to the project. You want the most rapid feedback on your changes. What should you do?

options.A: Apply the configuration to the production project and roll back if any resource fails to create.
options.B: Run a dry-run plan of the configuration, which resolves and reports the dependency graph without creating resources.
options.C: Create the resources manually in the console in dependency order to confirm the ordering is possible.
options.D: Commit the change and let the pipeline apply it to production, relying on monitoring alerts to detect failures.

explanation.summary: A dry-run plan resolves the full dependency graph and reports what would be created, changed or destroyed, without touching any real resource. That is both the fastest feedback loop and the only option that risks nothing.

option_breakdown.A: Applying to production to find out whether it works inverts the requirement: it is the slowest feedback and puts a live environment at risk.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The plan resolves dependencies and surfaces ordering or reference errors immediately, with no resources created.
option_breakdown.C: Manual console creation validates your ability to click in the right order, not the configuration, and leaves untracked resources behind.
option_breakdown.D: Committing first and relying on alerts makes production the test environment, and feedback arrives long after the change.

questions.title: Deletion protection stops an accidental instance delete
questions.summary: Enabling deletion protection on a Compute Engine instance makes the delete API call fail outright until the flag is explicitly cleared, guarding against a stray click or script.
questions.question: You are deploying a production application on a Compute Engine instance and want to prevent anyone from accidentally destroying it by clicking the wrong button. What should you do?

options.A: Enable deletion protection on the instance
options.B: Remove the delete permission from every IAM role in the project
options.C: Move the instance into its own project that nobody else has access to
options.D: Take a daily snapshot so the instance can be quickly recreated if deleted

explanation.summary: Deletion protection is a per-instance flag that causes any delete attempt — console, gcloud, or API — to fail until the flag is turned off first, which is a direct, low-effort guard against exactly the accidental-click scenario described.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the purpose-built safeguard for preventing accidental deletion of a specific instance, with no effect on anyone's other permissions.
option_breakdown.B: Stripping delete from every role would also block legitimate, intentional deletions across the whole project — a blunt, disruptive overreach for protecting one instance.
option_breakdown.C: Isolating the instance into its own project changes who can reach it at all, which may not be practical for a shared production workload, and doesn't itself prevent deletion by whoever does have access.
