option_breakdown.D: A snapshot enables recovery after a deletion but does nothing to prevent the deletion (and the resulting downtime) from happening in the first place.

questions.title: Running cleanup logic before a VM terminates
questions.summary: A shutdown-script metadata key runs on a best-effort basis right before an instance stops, resets, or is preempted, mirroring startup-script for the opposite end of the instance lifecycle.
questions.question: You are running a fleet of Spot VMs and want each instance to drain in-flight requests from the load balancer and flush a local buffer to Cloud Storage in the seconds before it is preempted. How should you implement this?

options.A: Poll the instance's maintenance-event metadata endpoint continuously from within the application and build all cleanup logic yourself around that signal
options.B: This is not possible — Spot VMs are terminated without any opportunity to run cleanup code
options.C: Add a shutdown-script metadata key whose script Compute Engine runs on a best-effort basis when the instance is stopped, reset, or preempted
options.D: Configure a Cloud Function triggered on the instance's deletion Admin Activity log entry to perform the cleanup remotely

explanation.summary: A shutdown-script metadata entry is the documented mechanism for exactly this: a script Compute Engine attempts to run before shutdown, stop, reset, or preemption, on a best-effort basis within a short time budget.

option_breakdown.A: Polling the maintenance-event endpoint is a real, complementary technique for detecting an imminent preemption early, but it is not the direct, built-in answer to 'run cleanup code right before termination' — that is what shutdown-script exists for.
option_breakdown.B: False — shutdown-script exists precisely to give best-effort cleanup time before termination, including preemption.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. This is the documented, purpose-built mechanism for pre-termination cleanup.
option_breakdown.D: A remote Cloud Function reacting after the fact cannot flush a local, in-memory buffer that only exists on the already-terminating instance — it has no access to that local state and arrives too late.

questions.title: Where the Spot provisioning option lives on VM creation
questions.summary: The VM provisioning model — Standard, Spot, or the legacy Preemptible flag — is set in the Availability policy section of the VM creation form, distinct from Identity/API access, Sole tenancy, and Networking.
questions.question: You're creating a VM through Cloud Console and want to run it as a Spot VM to cut cost. In which section of the create-instance page do you set this?

options.A: Availability policy
options.B: Identity and API access
options.C: Sole tenancy
options.D: Networking

explanation.summary: The Availability policy section controls the provisioning model — Standard, Spot, or the older Preemptible — along with related settings like on-host maintenance and automatic restart.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is where the provisioning model is set.
option_breakdown.B: Identity and API access controls which service account the VM runs as and its access scopes — unrelated to provisioning model.
option_breakdown.C: Sole tenancy is about running your VMs on a physical server dedicated only to your workloads, a separate concern from Spot pricing.
option_breakdown.D: Networking configures the VPC, subnet, and network interfaces, not the provisioning or billing model.

questions.title: Adding a second network interface to a new VM
questions.summary: A second network interface for a VM is configured on the Networking tab of the create-instance form — each interface attaches to a different VPC network, and Compute Engine still assigns its IP automatically unless overridden there.
questions.question: You're creating a VM that needs interfaces on two separate VPC networks. Where in the Cloud Console create-instance flow do you add the second network interface?

options.A: It isn't possible — GCP sets a VM's IP address automatically and doesn't allow manual interface configuration
options.B: On the Networking tab, where you can add another network interface bound to a different VPC network
options.C: In a separate Cloud Router configuration step, which precedes VM creation
options.D: By editing firewall rules for the target VPC network

explanation.summary: The Networking tab is where additional network interfaces are added at creation time, each bound to a distinct VPC network.

option_breakdown.A: Automatic IP assignment is the default, not a restriction — it doesn't prevent adding more interfaces, and each interface can still be given a manual IP if needed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Router handles dynamic route exchange, e.g. for VPN or Interconnect — it has no role in attaching interfaces to a VM.
option_breakdown.D: Firewall rules control traffic to and from interfaces that already exist; they don't create new interfaces.

questions.title: Autoscaler initialization period, not the health-check timeout
questions.summary: A Managed Instance Group's autoscaler judges new instances' utilization once its initialization period expires; when that period is shorter than a VM's real warm-up time, the autoscaler counts a not-yet-ready instance as still overloaded and keeps adding more.
questions.question: Your Managed Instance Group autoscales on CPU utilization above 80%, capped at five VMs. Instances take about three minutes to become ready, but you observe the group repeatedly scales up past the traffic level actually warrants before settling back down. What should you do?

options.A: Increase the autoscaler's initialization period to roughly match how long an instance actually takes to become ready, for example 200 seconds
options.B: Lower the CPU utilization target so the autoscaler reacts to load sooner
options.C: Increase the maximum group size so there is more headroom during the ramp-up window
options.D: Switch to manual scaling and add instances by hand whenever utilization spikes

explanation.summary: During a VM's boot and application warm-up, its reported CPU utilization is misleadingly high; the autoscaler's initialization period is meant to ignore metrics from a new instance until it's actually settled, so setting that window shorter than real warm-up time makes the autoscaler misread not-ready instances as overloaded and pile on more than necessary.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Aligning the initialization period with real warm-up time stops the autoscaler from judging a still-booting instance's noisy early metrics, removing the over-provisioning behavior.
option_breakdown.B: A lower target makes the autoscaler trigger even more eagerly, worsening the over-scaling symptom rather than fixing its root cause.
option_breakdown.C: More headroom just gives the same misbehaving logic more instances to over-provision into — it doesn't address why the autoscaler is over-reacting in the first place.
option_breakdown.D: Abandoning autoscaling entirely trades one problem for a worse one: no automated response to real traffic changes at all.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling MIG_NAME --zone=ZONE --cool-down-period=200 --target-cpu-utilization=0.8

questions.title: Spanner's built-in autoscaler, not a hand-rolled one
questions.summary: Cloud Spanner ships a native autoscaling feature that adjusts compute capacity to load automatically, replacing the older pattern of a Monitoring alert wired to a custom Cloud Function that resized the instance.
questions.question: Your application uses Cloud Spanner as its backend database, with a predictable but variable traffic pattern. You want Spanner's compute capacity to scale up and down automatically with that traffic, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Enable Cloud Spanner's built-in autoscaling on the instance, setting minimum and maximum processing units
options.B: Create a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy on Spanner CPU that calls a webhook, and write a Cloud Function that resizes the instance in response
options.C: Manually resize the Spanner instance at the start and end of each predictable traffic window
options.D: Migrate to Cloud SQL, since Spanner has no capacity-scaling mechanism at all

explanation.summary: Spanner instance autoscaling is a native, Google-managed feature that continuously adjusts processing units within configured bounds to track load — it directly replaces the older custom-automation pattern of alerting to a Cloud Function, which now carries needless operational risk and lag.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The native autoscaler is purpose-built for exactly this requirement and needs no custom code or webhook plumbing to operate or maintain.
option_breakdown.B: A hand-rolled Cloud Function reacting to an alert is the pattern the native autoscaler was introduced to replace — it adds maintenance burden, alerting lag, and a custom failure mode for a solved problem.
option_breakdown.C: Manual resizing does not scale to actual real-time traffic and requires ongoing human intervention that automation should handle.
option_breakdown.D: Spanner does have a capacity-scaling mechanism (both manual and now native autoscaling); this claim is simply incorrect, and migrating databases is a drastic, unwarranted response.

questions.title: Local SSD when a Persistent Disk throttles read throughput
questions.summary: When large sequential reads are hitting a Zonal Persistent Disk's throughput ceiling, moving the workload to Local SSD raises that ceiling dramatically while remaining the cheaper option for this access pattern.
questions.question: An application on a general-purpose Compute Engine instance reads large files primarily from a 350-GB Zonal SSD Persistent Disk, and you observe excessive disk read throttling. You want maximum throughput while minimizing cost. What should you do?

options.A: Migrate the workload's data onto a Local SSD attached to the instance
options.B: Increase the Persistent Disk's size without changing its type, since larger disks always get more throughput
options.C: Switch the boot disk to Standard (HDD) Persistent Disk to free up IOPS headroom
options.D: Add more vCPUs to the instance so it can process reads faster

explanation.summary: Local SSD offers far higher per-instance throughput and IOPS than any Persistent Disk tier, at a lower per-GB price than SSD Persistent Disk — a strong match for a large-sequential-read workload that is bottlenecked on disk throughput, not the machine's compute.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Local SSD directly raises the throughput ceiling this workload is hitting, at lower cost than continuing to scale up SSD Persistent Disk capacity to chase more throughput.
option_breakdown.B: Persistent Disk throughput does scale with provisioned size up to a per-instance cap, but chasing that ceiling by over-provisioning capacity you don't need is a more expensive way to reach lower throughput than Local SSD offers directly.
option_breakdown.C: Standard HDD Persistent Disk has lower throughput and higher latency than SSD Persistent Disk — this makes the read-throttling problem worse, not better.
option_breakdown.D: The bottleneck described is disk read throughput, not CPU — adding vCPUs does nothing to relieve a storage I/O ceiling.

questions.title: SSH to one instance for one group
questions.summary: OS Login with the role bound at instance scope confines access to that one instance.
questions.question: You want to configure SSH access to a single Compute Engine instance for users in the dev1 group. This instance is the only resource in the project that dev1 users should be able to connect to. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the group a project-level Compute role.
options.B: Add the group members' SSH keys to project-wide metadata.
options.C: Enable OS Login on the instance and grant the group the OS Login role on that instance only.
options.D: Create a firewall rule allowing SSH from the group's IP addresses.

explanation.summary: OS Login ties Linux logins to IAM identities, and binding roles/compute.osLogin on the instance resource rather than the project confines access to exactly that instance.

option_breakdown.A: A project-level grant reaches every instance in the project, which over-grants when only one instance should be reachable.
option_breakdown.B: Project-wide metadata keys reach every instance in the project and are not tied to IAM identities or revoked on offboarding.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. OS Login ties Linux logins to IAM identities, and binding roles/compute.osLogin on the instance resource rather than the project confines access to exactly that instance.
option_breakdown.D: A firewall rule controls network reachability only; it authorises no user and grants no login.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances add-metadata dev-vm --zone=us-central1-a \
  --metadata enable-oslogin=TRUE
gcloud compute instances add-iam-policy-binding dev-vm --zone=us-central1-a \
  --member='group:dev1@example.com' --role='roles/compute.osLogin'

questions.title: Shared-key SSH replaced by attributable admin login
questions.summary: compute.osAdminLogin grants sudo-capable SSH bound to each person's own Google identity, so a whole team gets root without ever sharing a credential.
questions.question: Every employee at your company has a Google account. Your operations team needs administrative SSH access to a large number of Compute Engine instances. Your security team wants credential deployment to be operationally efficient and wants to be able to determine who accessed a given instance. What should you do?

options.A: Have each operator upload their SSH public key to every instance's metadata individually
options.B: Enable OS Login on the project, and grant the operations team's Google group the roles/compute.osAdminLogin role
options.C: Enable OS Login on the project, and grant the operations team's Google group the roles/compute.osLogin role
options.D: Share a single root SSH key pair among the operations team and rotate it monthly

explanation.summary: OS Login maps each Google identity to its own POSIX account server-side, so granting osAdminLogin to the team's group gives every member sudo access under their own name — no per-instance key management and a per-user audit trail.

option_breakdown.A: Per-instance metadata keys mean re-uploading a key to every VM and re-uploading it again on every new instance — the opposite of operationally efficient.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. osAdminLogin is the sudo-capable OS Login role, and binding it once to a group scales to any number of instances and any team size.
option_breakdown.C: Plain osLogin grants SSH but not administrative (sudo) rights, which this team needs.
option_breakdown.D: A shared credential makes every login indistinguishable — it directly defeats the 'determine who accessed a given instance' requirement.

questions.title: Shielded VM defends against rootkits and bootkits
questions.summary: Shielded VM bundles Secure Boot, a virtual TPM, and Integrity Monitoring to verify a VM's boot chain hasn't been tampered with — the direct control against rootkits and other boot- or kernel-level malware, unrelated to firewalls or SSH key management.
questions.question: You're hardening a new production VM and specifically want protection against an attacker injecting a rootkit that alters the operating system at the boot or kernel level. Which Compute Engine option should you enable when creating the VM?

options.A: A firewall rule restricting inbound traffic to the instance
options.B: Shielded VM, which adds Secure Boot, a virtual TPM, and integrity monitoring to verify the boot chain
options.C: Project-wide SSH keys for consistent administrator access
options.D: A more restrictive IAM role on the instance's service account

explanation.summary: Shielded VM's Secure Boot, vTPM, and Integrity Monitoring are specifically designed to detect and prevent boot- and kernel-level tampering such as rootkits and bootkits — none of the other options touch the boot chain at all.

option_breakdown.A: Firewall rules control network traffic in and out of the instance; they have no visibility into what's happening inside the boot process.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. This is exactly what Shielded VM is designed to protect against.
option_breakdown.C: Project-wide SSH keys are an access-management convenience with no relationship to boot integrity.
option_breakdown.D: A tighter service-account role limits what the VM's identity can do against Google Cloud APIs — it does nothing to detect tampering with the guest OS itself.

questions.title: A custom query quota caps runaway BigQuery spend
questions.summary: A user- or project-level custom query quota puts a hard ceiling on bytes billed per day, directly controlling BigQuery on-demand cost rather than reacting to it after the fact.
questions.question: Your company runs BigQuery as an enterprise data warehouse, and users across multiple business units query it. Query costs have become very high and you need to control them proactively. What should you do?

options.C: Apply a user- or project-level custom query quota that caps bytes billed per day
options.D: Wait for the monthly bill and email teams whose queries were most expensive
options.A: Disable BigQuery access for all business units except one
options.B: Switch every table to a smaller storage class to reduce query cost

explanation.summary: A custom quota is enforced at query time — once a user or project has billed the configured number of bytes for the day, further on-demand queries are blocked, which is a hard proactive cost control rather than a retrospective report.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This directly bounds the cost driver (bytes scanned) before the spend happens, for exactly the users or projects you scope it to.
option_breakdown.D: An after-the-fact email is a detective control, not a preventive one — it does nothing to cap the spend that already happened.
option_breakdown.A: Cutting off access entirely removes the cost but also removes the legitimate warehouse access every other team needs.
option_breakdown.B: Storage class governs storage cost, not query cost — BigQuery's on-demand pricing is based on bytes scanned per query, unrelated to which storage tier the table sits in (and BigQuery does not expose Cloud Storage storage classes for its own tables regardless).

explanation.gcloud_command:
# Console > IAM & Admin > Quotas: set 'Query usage per day' (project) and
# 'Query usage per day per user' for the BigQuery API to a byte ceiling

questions.title: Dry-run a BigQuery query to price it before running it
questions.summary: A dry-run query returns the bytes a query would scan without actually running or billing it, letting you convert that estimate to dollars before committing to an expensive on-demand query.
questions.question: You need to run an important BigQuery query that you expect will return a lot of records, and you're on on-demand pricing. You want to find out how much the query will cost before running it. What should you do?

options.C: Run the query with the dry-run flag to estimate the number of bytes it will read, then convert that to a dollar estimate using the published on-demand price per byte
options.D: Run the query once fully, note the cost on the invoice, and decide afterward whether it was worth it
options.A: Manually count the rows in every table referenced by the query and multiply by an assumed row size
options.B: Switch the project to flat-rate pricing first, since only flat-rate exposes a cost estimate

explanation.summary: A dry run validates and plans the query without executing it or scanning any billable bytes, and returns the exact number of bytes the real run would process — multiplying that by BigQuery's per-TB on-demand price gives an accurate cost estimate before you spend anything.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This is the documented, zero-cost way to find out what a query will cost before actually running and paying for it.
option_breakdown.D: Running the query first to learn its cost defeats the purpose of estimating beforehand — by then you've already paid for it.
option_breakdown.A: Manually estimating row counts and sizes ignores how BigQuery actually bills (bytes scanned in the referenced columns, not row count), and is far less accurate and far more effort than a dry run.
option_breakdown.B: Dry-run estimation works under on-demand pricing specifically (that's exactly what determines cost-per-byte); flat-rate pricing is a capacity subscription and isn't required, or even relevant, to get a bytes estimate.

questions.title: Snapshots only charge for the incremental delta after the first
questions.summary: Persistent disk snapshots are incremental: the first snapshot of a disk stores a full copy, and every later snapshot from that disk stores only the delta since the previous one — so billed snapshot storage tracks changed data, not repeated full copies.
questions.question: You snapshot a 100 GB persistent disk, then add 10 GB of new data to it, then take a second snapshot. Assuming no compression, how much total snapshot storage are you billed for?

options.A: 210 GB — each snapshot bills for the full 100 GB disk, plus the second capturing the extra 10 GB
options.B: 110 GB — the first snapshot bills for the full 100 GB, and the second bills only for the 10 GB that changed
options.C: 110 GB, but the first snapshot is deleted automatically once the second is created
options.D: 221 GB — the two snapshot sizes plus a 10 percent metadata overhead surcharge on the second

explanation.summary: Compute Engine snapshots are incremental after the first: the initial snapshot for a disk stores a full copy, and every subsequent snapshot from that disk stores only the changed blocks since the previous snapshot — so total billed storage is 100 GB + 10 GB = 110 GB, with no automatic deletion and no metadata surcharge.

option_breakdown.A: This treats both snapshots as full copies; only the first snapshot of a disk is a full copy.
option_breakdown.B: Correct — only the changed 10 GB is billed for the second, incremental snapshot.
option_breakdown.C: Earlier snapshots aren't deleted automatically when a new one is taken; each remains independently restorable until you explicitly delete it.
option_breakdown.D: There is no metadata overhead surcharge added to incremental snapshot billing.

questions.title: Cloud SQL binary logging is the setup prerequisite for point-in-time recovery
questions.summary: Point-in-time recovery on Cloud SQL for MySQL depends on binary logging being enabled at provisioning time — a configuration decision, not something you can retrofit during a restore.
questions.question: You want to select and configure a cost-effective solution for relational data. You are working with a small set of operational data in one geographic location, and you need to support point-in-time recovery. What should you do?

options.C: Provision Cloud SQL for MySQL, and verify that the 'enable binary logging' option is selected
options.D: Provision Cloud SQL for MySQL with binary logging left at its default disabled state, and enable it later if a restore is ever needed
options.A: Provision Cloud Spanner and rely on its automatic multi-region replication for recovery
options.B: Provision BigQuery and use table snapshots for recovery

explanation.summary: Cloud SQL is the cost-effective fit for a small, single-region relational workload, and point-in-time recovery specifically requires binary logging to have been recording transactions all along — it cannot be turned on retroactively to cover a gap in the past.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud SQL matches the size and locality requirement, and enabling binary logging at setup is the prerequisite that makes PITR possible later.
option_breakdown.D: Leaving binary logging off means no PITR window exists when you eventually need one — the whole point is that it must already be running before the incident.
option_breakdown.A: Spanner is built for global horizontal scale and synchronous multi-region consistency, well beyond what a small single-location dataset needs, and is far from the cost-effective choice here.
option_breakdown.B: BigQuery is an analytics warehouse, not an OLTP relational database, and table snapshots are not equivalent to transaction-log-based point-in-time recovery.

questions.title: Serve PDFs inline with a Content-Type header
questions.summary: A browser decides whether to render or download a Cloud Storage object based on its Content-Type metadata, so setting it to application/pdf makes PDFs display inline instead of prompting a save dialog.
questions.question: You host a static website on Cloud Storage that links to PDF files. Currently, clicking a PDF link prompts the browser to save the file locally. You want the PDF to display inside the browser window instead, without a save prompt. What should you do?

options.D: Set the Content-Type metadata on the PDF objects to application/pdf
options.A: Move the PDF files into a separate bucket configured for static website hosting
options.B: Rename each file so it ends in .html instead of .pdf
options.C: Enable Cloud CDN in front of the bucket

explanation.summary: Browsers decide render-versus-download behavior largely from the HTTP Content-Type response header — objects lacking a correct type default to a generic download behavior, while application/pdf tells the browser to open its built-in PDF viewer inline.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. Setting the correct MIME type on the object metadata is exactly what controls this browser behavior.
option_breakdown.A: A second static-website bucket changes nothing about how an individual PDF object's headers are served.
option_breakdown.B: Renaming a PDF's extension to .html does not change its actual content type or bytes, and browsers will fail to render it as either format correctly.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud CDN caches responses at the edge for performance; it does not alter the Content-Type an object is served with.

questions.title: Lifecycle rule that only archives superseded object versions
questions.summary: An Object Lifecycle Management condition scoped to noncurrent (isLive: false) versions moves only superseded copies to a cheaper class, leaving the live version untouched for ongoing edits.
questions.question: You want a cost-effective archiving policy for a versioned Cloud Storage bucket. Data with newer versions should move to Nearline after 30 days. Old versions are accessed about once a month for reporting, and the current version is occasionally updated at month-end. What should you do?

options.D: Add a bucket lifecycle rule scoped to noncurrent versions (isLive: false) that transitions them to Nearline Storage after 30 days
options.A: Add a bucket lifecycle rule that transitions every object, live or noncurrent, to Nearline Storage after 30 days
options.B: Disable Object Versioning so there is only ever one copy to manage
options.C: Manually move superseded objects to a separate archive bucket each month

explanation.summary: Scoping the rule to noncurrent versions means only objects that already have a newer version get archived, leaving the live version at Standard class so it stays cheap and fast to keep updating, matching both the monthly access pattern for old versions and the occasional month-end edits.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. This condition targets exactly 'data with newer versions,' as stated, while leaving the current version untouched.
option_breakdown.A: Transitioning the live version too would move actively-edited data into Nearline, which carries a 30-day minimum storage charge and no benefit for data still being updated.
option_breakdown.B: Disabling versioning removes the ability to distinguish current from historical data at all, breaking the reporting use of old versions.
option_breakdown.C: A manual monthly process is exactly the operational overhead that lifecycle rules exist to automate away, and is easy to forget or get wrong.

questions.title: Skip straight to Archive after the 30-day active window
questions.summary: When an object is read heavily for a short active window and then almost never again, a lifecycle rule can transition straight from Standard to Archive, skipping the intermediate classes entirely.
questions.question: You need Object Lifecycle Management for objects that are written once and read frequently for the first 30 days. After that, they are essentially never read again except for rare special requests, and must be retained for three years total. You want to minimize cost. What should you do?

options.D: Set up a lifecycle rule that uses Standard storage for the first 30 days, then transitions directly to Archive Storage for the remaining term
options.A: Set up a lifecycle rule that transitions Standard to Nearline after 30 days, then to Coldline after 90 days, then to Archive after a year
options.B: Keep every object in Standard storage for the full three years to avoid any retrieval fees
options.C: Move objects to Coldline after 30 days and keep them there for the full three years

explanation.summary: The intermediate classes exist to price data that is read occasionally over its life; here access essentially stops after day 30, so paying the lower Archive storage rate immediately — rather than stepping down through Nearline and Coldline's higher rates first — minimizes cost over the full three-year retention.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. Because reads effectively stop after 30 days, jumping straight to Archive's lowest storage price is cheaper than lingering in the pricier intermediate classes on the way there.
option_breakdown.A: Stepping through Nearline and Coldline first means paying their higher per-GB rates for months before reaching Archive, for data that is already barely being read by day 30.
option_breakdown.B: Standard class carries the highest storage price of all the classes — appropriate for the first 30 days of frequent reads, but needlessly expensive to hold for three years of near-zero access.
option_breakdown.C: Coldline is priced for roughly quarterly access; 'essentially never read' for the bulk of three years is well past that threshold, so Archive's lower storage price wins.

questions.title: Join a Spanner export and Bigtable through federated BigQuery tables
questions.summary: BigQuery external tables can query Cloud Storage exports and Cloud Bigtable directly, so an ad hoc cross-database join needs no ETL pipeline — just two external table definitions and one SQL statement.
questions.question: Your application uses Cloud Spanner for current user state and Cloud Bigtable for a log of user events, and you export Spanner data to Cloud Storage during daily backups. An analyst needs to join data from both sources for specific users, as an efficient one-off request. What should you do?

options.D: Create a BigQuery external table over the Cloud Storage export and a BigQuery external table over Cloud Bigtable, then join them with a single SQL query
options.A: Write a Dataflow pipeline that reads from both sources, joins the records, and writes the result to a new BigQuery table
options.B: Export Bigtable to Cloud Storage as well, then manually diff the two exported files with a spreadsheet
options.C: Set up a permanent Dataproc cluster to run a scheduled Spark job that joins the two datasets nightly

explanation.summary: Both Cloud Storage and Cloud Bigtable are natively queryable as BigQuery external tables, so a single ad hoc SQL query can join across them directly — no pipeline needs to be built, run or maintained for a one-off analytical request.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. Two external table definitions and one JOIN accomplish the task with no data movement and no pipeline to build.
option_breakdown.A: A full Dataflow pipeline is real engineering effort for a use case explicitly described as ad hoc and one-off — the external-table approach gets the same answer in minutes.
option_breakdown.B: Manually diffing exported files in a spreadsheet does not scale past a handful of rows and throws away SQL's join capability entirely.
option_breakdown.C: A permanent scheduled cluster is ongoing infrastructure for a single ad hoc request — far more than the task requires, and the opposite of 'as efficiently as possible.'

questions.title: Two lifecycle actions, two independent age thresholds
questions.summary: One Object Lifecycle Management policy can carry multiple independent rules, each with its own age condition, so a single bucket can both change storage class at 90 days and delete at 365 days.
questions.question: You need videos in a Regional Cloud Storage bucket to move to Coldline after 90 days, and to be deleted entirely one year after their creation date. How should you set up the policy?

options.D: Configure a lifecycle policy with two Age-based rules: a SetStorageClass action to Coldline at 90 days, and a separate Delete action at 365 days
options.A: Configure a single lifecycle rule with one Age condition that both changes the storage class and deletes the object at 90 days
options.B: Configure a lifecycle rule that deletes the object at 90 days, then manually re-upload a Coldline copy that expires at 365 days
options.C: Configure two separate buckets — one Coldline, one Standard — and move objects between them with a script

explanation.summary: Object Lifecycle Management evaluates each rule in the policy independently against every object, so a SetStorageClass rule at 90 days and an unrelated Delete rule at 365 days coexist cleanly, each firing at its own threshold with no interaction required between them.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. Two independent age-based rules produce exactly the two required behaviors at exactly the two required thresholds, entirely automatically.
option_breakdown.A: One condition cannot express two different actions at two different ages — deleting at 90 days would destroy the video well before the required one-year retention.
option_breakdown.B: Deleting and manually re-uploading not only adds needless manual work, it also destroys the object at 90 days instead of retaining it, which contradicts the requirement.
option_breakdown.C: Managing a custom script to move objects between two buckets duplicates functionality that a single lifecycle policy already provides natively and reliably.

questions.title: Routes Google creates automatically in an auto mode VPC
questions.summary: An auto mode VPC gets a default 0.0.0.0/0 internet route at creation, plus one implicit subnet route per region as each auto subnet is added — routes you never author by hand.
questions.question: You create a brand-new VPC network in auto mode and add no custom routes. Without any manual configuration, what routing already exists in this network?

options.A: No routes exist until at least one firewall rule is created
options.B: Only a single route exists, covering the network's default subnet in us-central1
options.C: A default route for internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0), plus one implicit route per subnet, created automatically as each regional subnet is added
options.D: Routes are created only after a Cloud Router is attached to the network

explanation.summary: Auto mode creates a default internet route with the network itself, and Google automatically generates one subnet route per region as it creates that region's auto subnet — matching the network's full regional footprint from the start.

option_breakdown.A: Routes and firewall rules are independent concepts; implicit routes exist regardless of firewall state.
option_breakdown.B: Auto mode creates a subnet in every region, not just one, and each gets its own automatic route.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Both the default internet route and per-subnet routes are created automatically with no manual step.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Router is for dynamic BGP routing over VPN or Interconnect; it is unrelated to these baseline implicit routes.

questions.title: Resizing a VM's memory requires a stop first
questions.summary: Changing a running Compute Engine instance's machine type — including its memory allocation — requires stopping the instance first; it cannot be resized live.
questions.question: You have a Compute Engine VM configured with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of memory, and it is running out of memory. You want to upgrade it to 8 GB of memory. What should you do?

options.A: Stop the VM, change its machine type to one with 8 GB of memory, then start the VM
options.B: Edit the memory value while the VM keeps running; Compute Engine applies it on the fly
options.C: Attach an additional persistent disk formatted as swap space to simulate the extra memory
options.D: Create a second VM with more memory and manually copy the running processes over

explanation.summary: A machine type change — vCPU count, memory, or both — is only accepted while the instance is stopped; Compute Engine rejects the change on a running instance, so the stop-change-start sequence is mandatory, not optional.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the required, and only supported, sequence for changing a running instance's memory allocation.
option_breakdown.B: Compute Engine has no live-resize capability for machine type — attempting to change it while running is rejected by the API.
option_breakdown.C: Swap space on a persistent disk is dramatically slower than RAM and does not address the application's actual memory shortage — it's a workaround, not the requested upgrade.
option_breakdown.D: Manually migrating running processes between VMs is operationally fragile and far more disruptive than a brief, supported stop-and-resize.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instances stop INSTANCE_NAME --zone=ZONE && gcloud compute instances set-machine-type INSTANCE_NAME --zone=ZONE --machine-type=e2-standard-2 && gcloud compute instances start INSTANCE_NAME --zone=ZONE

questions.title: Kubernetes Secret keeps a database password out of plaintext
questions.summary: A Kubernetes Secret object stores the value out of the plain YAML manifest, and the Pod spec references it by name so the password never appears in version control.
questions.question: You deployed a microservice to a GKE cluster with the database password written directly as plain text in the YAML manifest. You need to refactor this so the password is not stored in plain text, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Store the password inside a Kubernetes Secret object, and populate the DB_PASSWORD environment variable from that Secret in the Pod spec
options.B: Base64-encode the password and paste the encoded string directly into the YAML manifest in place of the plaintext value
options.C: Move the password into a ConfigMap, and reference the ConfigMap from the Pod spec
options.D: Store the password in an environment variable set on each GKE node's underlying VM

explanation.summary: A Secret is the Kubernetes-native object for sensitive values: it is stored separately from the Pod manifest, access is governed by RBAC, and the manifest itself only references it by name — the password text never needs to appear in version-controlled YAML.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the standard Kubernetes mechanism for keeping sensitive values out of plaintext manifests, and it integrates cleanly with environment-variable injection.
option_breakdown.B: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption — anyone who can read the manifest can trivially decode it, so this does not actually address the plaintext-exposure problem.
option_breakdown.C: A ConfigMap is explicitly designed for non-sensitive configuration data and offers none of a Secret's tighter RBAC and handling protections — it is the wrong object type for a password.
option_breakdown.D: A node-level environment variable is visible to every Pod scheduled on that node and is not how workload-scoped credentials should be delivered in Kubernetes.

questions.title: Fetch Windows RDP credentials with one gcloud command
questions.summary: gcloud compute reset-windows-password sets and returns a fresh Windows username and password in one step, ready to use in an RDP client immediately.
questions.question: You are setting up a Windows VM on Compute Engine and want to be able to log in via RDP. What should you do?

options.A: After the VM is created, run gcloud compute reset-windows-password to retrieve login credentials
options.B: SSH into the VM first, then run a PowerShell script to create a new local Windows account
options.C: Wait for Compute Engine to email the default administrator password automatically
options.D: Rebuild the VM from a Linux image, since RDP requires Linux-native remote desktop support

explanation.summary: reset-windows-password creates or resets a local Windows account through the guest agent and prints a fresh, ready-to-use username and password — the direct, documented path to your first RDP login.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This one command produces working RDP credentials with no manual account setup.
option_breakdown.B: SSH is not available on Windows VMs by default, and this path is far more manual than the built-in password-reset command.
option_breakdown.C: Compute Engine never emails credentials automatically — you must explicitly request them.
option_breakdown.D: RDP is the Windows remote-desktop protocol; rebuilding as Linux would remove Windows (and RDP) entirely, the opposite of the goal.

questions.title: A Pending Pod recovering from node preemption
questions.summary: A Pod stuck in Pending shortly after a Deployment on a preemptible node pool is often just being rescheduled after its original node was preempted — a transient, self-resolving state rather than a persistent scheduling failure.
questions.question: You create a Deployment with 2 replicas on a GKE cluster that has a single node pool of Spot (preemptible) VMs. A few minutes later, kubectl shows one Pod still in Pending status. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The Pod's original node was preempted between the Deployment's creation and your status check, and the Pod is currently being rescheduled onto a new node
options.B: The cluster has permanently run out of schedulable capacity and will never place the Pod
options.C: The Deployment's YAML contains a syntax error that is silently blocking the second replica
options.D: GKE does not support running Deployments on preemptible node pools at all

explanation.summary: Preemptible nodes can be reclaimed by Compute Engine at any time with short notice; a Pod that was running on a just-preempted node briefly shows Pending while the scheduler places it on another available node — this resolves on its own without intervention.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the expected, transient behavior of workloads on preemptible capacity, and describe events for the Pod would show a preemption-related eviction shortly before the Pending state.
option_breakdown.B: A genuinely exhausted cluster would show a persistent scheduling failure in the Pod's events (insufficient CPU/memory), not simply resolve moments after Deployment creation as this transient case does.
option_breakdown.C: A YAML syntax error would be rejected by the API server at apply time (or produce a consistent, non-transient failure), not a Pod that briefly sits Pending and then schedules normally.
option_breakdown.D: GKE fully supports running workloads, including Deployments, on preemptible node pools — this is a common, supported cost-optimization pattern.

questions.title: Cloud Run min-instances 0 for a business-hours internal app
questions.summary: Setting minimum instances to zero on a fully managed Cloud Run service accepts occasional cold starts in exchange for paying nothing while the app sits idle outside business hours.
questions.question: You developed a containerized web application for internal colleagues, used only during business hours. You want zero cost incurred outside those hours, in a freshly created project. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy the container on Cloud Run (fully managed) with minimum instances set to zero
options.B: Deploy the container on Cloud Run (fully managed) with minimum instances set to one
options.C: Deploy the container on a Compute Engine VM, and stop the VM manually at the end of each business day
options.D: Deploy the container on GKE Autopilot with a single always-on replica

explanation.summary: Cloud Run bills only while a container instance is actively handling requests; min-instances=0 lets it scale all the way down to nothing outside business hours, accepting a cold start on the next request in exchange for zero idle cost.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the direct configuration for 'no cost while idle' — the tradeoff (an occasional cold start) is acceptable for an internal, non-latency-critical tool.
option_breakdown.B: min-instances=1 keeps one instance warm around the clock, which means paying for it outside business hours too — the opposite of the stated cost goal.
option_breakdown.C: Manually stopping a VM every evening is an ongoing operational chore that Cloud Run's automatic scale-to-zero eliminates entirely.
option_breakdown.D: An always-on GKE replica bills continuously regardless of business hours, the same idle-cost problem as option B, with more infrastructure to manage besides.

questions.title: Shipping 10GB of reference data to every new VM
questions.summary: For a modest, unchanging dataset that every new VM needs at boot, baking it into a custom image and using that image as the source when creating each VM is simpler and faster than copying the data at boot time from Cloud Storage.
questions.question: A data scientist needs the same 10 GB reference dataset available on the local filesystem of every new analysis VM the team spins up. What's the most efficient way to provide this?

options.A: Have each VM's startup script copy the dataset from Cloud Storage on every boot
options.B: Create a disk image containing the dataset, and use it as the source image when creating each VM
options.C: Have engineers manually copy the dataset onto each new VM after it's created
options.D: Load the dataset into a database and have each VM query it remotely

explanation.summary: Since the dataset is small and static, baking it into a custom image means every new VM has it immediately at boot, with no copy step at all.

option_breakdown.A: Works, but re-copies the same 10 GB from Cloud Storage on every boot — wasted time and egress compared to baking it in once.
option_breakdown.B: Correct.
option_breakdown.C: Manual copying doesn't scale and reintroduces exactly the kind of undocumented, error-prone process good practice avoids.
option_breakdown.D: The requirement is a local filesystem copy, not a queryable database — this changes the access pattern the analysis tooling expects.

questions.title: Custom images can be built from disks, snapshots, or images
questions.summary: Custom images can be created from a persistent disk, a snapshot, another image, or a Cloud Storage RAW disk file — of the four multiple-choice options given, disks/snapshots/images is the most complete, since a database export file is never a valid source.
questions.question: A custom Compute Engine image can be created from which of the following sources?

options.A: Only an existing disk
options.B: A snapshot or a disk only
options.C: A disk, a snapshot, or another existing image
options.D: A disk, a snapshot, or any database export file

explanation.summary: Disks, snapshots, and other images are all valid image sources. Compute Engine additionally supports a Cloud Storage RAW file as a source, which none of these four options capture, making option C the most complete of the choices offered.

option_breakdown.A: Too narrow — snapshots and other images are valid sources too.
option_breakdown.B: Still too narrow — it omits creating an image directly from another image.
option_breakdown.C: Correct among the given options — disks, snapshots, and other images are all valid sources.
option_breakdown.D: A database export file (e.g., a SQL dump) is never a valid image source.

questions.title: Deprecating an image flags it and points to a replacement
questions.summary: Deprecating an image marks it as no longer the recommended choice — optionally pointing at a specific replacement image — while leaving it usable; the image isn't deleted, and Compute Engine's real state names are ACTIVE, DEPRECATED, and OBSOLETE.
questions.question: You've built newer images on Ubuntu 20.04 and want to steer users away from your older Ubuntu 18.04 images without deleting them outright. Which image feature accomplishes this?

options.A: Redirection
options.B: Deprecation, optionally naming a replacement image
options.C: Marking the image unsupported
options.D: Migration

explanation.summary: Deprecation is exactly this: flag the image, optionally reference a --replacement, and keep it usable in the meantime — it isn't deleted and isn't guaranteed to keep receiving security patches.

option_breakdown.A: Redirection isn't an image lifecycle feature in Compute Engine.
option_breakdown.B: Correct — deprecation flags the image and can name a replacement, without deleting it.
option_breakdown.C: Compute Engine's actual state names are ACTIVE, DEPRECATED, and OBSOLETE — 'unsupported' isn't one of them.
option_breakdown.D: Migration isn't an image feature; it describes a broader process, not an image state.

questions.title: List instance inventory as JSON with --format=json
questions.summary: gcloud compute instances list enumerates every instance, and its output format is controlled with --format — --format=json is the correct flag; there's no --output flag, and describe targets one instance rather than the whole inventory.
questions.question: You want a JSON-formatted inventory of every VM in your project. Which gcloud command produces that?

options.A: gcloud compute instances list
options.B: gcloud compute instances describe
options.C: gcloud compute instances list --format=json
options.D: gcloud compute instances list --output=json

explanation.summary: --format=json is gcloud's standard formatting flag, applied here to the list command; plain list defaults to a human-readable table, describe targets a single instance, and --output isn't a valid gcloud flag.

option_breakdown.A: list without a format flag prints human-readable table output, not JSON.
option_breakdown.B: describe returns detail on one named instance, not an inventory of every VM.
option_breakdown.C: Correct — --format=json is gcloud's standard formatting flag, applied here to the list command.
option_breakdown.D: --output isn't a valid gcloud flag; the flag is --format.

questions.title: --keep-disks=boot preserves the boot disk on instance deletion
questions.summary: The real flag is --keep-disks, with valid values boot, data, or all — 'filesystem' isn't a valid value, and there's no --save-disks flag.
questions.question: You're deleting ch06-instance-1 but want to keep its boot disk while letting any other attached disks be removed. Which command does this?

options.A: gcloud compute instances delete ch06-instance-1 --keep-disks=boot
options.B: gcloud compute instances delete ch06-instance-1 --save-disks=boot
options.C: gcloud compute instances delete ch06-instance-1 --keep-disks=filesystem
options.D: gcloud compute delete ch06-instance-1 --keep-disks=filesystem

explanation.summary: --keep-disks=boot is the exact valid flag and value for preserving only the boot disk on delete; 'filesystem' isn't a valid --keep-disks value and --save-disks doesn't exist.

option_breakdown.A: Correct — --keep-disks=boot is the exact valid flag and value for this.
option_breakdown.B: --save-disks isn't a real gcloud flag.
option_breakdown.C: 'filesystem' isn't a valid --keep-disks value (valid values are boot, data, all).
option_breakdown.D: Missing the 'instances' resource noun, and repeats the invalid 'filesystem' value.

questions.title: Email when VM CPU exceeds 90 percent
questions.summary: An alerting policy with a duration window on the exported CPU metric, wired to an email channel.
questions.question: You have a Compute Engine instance hosting a production application and want to receive an email if the instance consumes more than 90% of its CPU for more than 15 minutes, using Google services only. What should you do?

options.A: Install and configure the Ops Agent on the instances.
options.B: Create an alerting policy on the metric with a notification channel.
options.C: Create a log-based metric from a Cloud Logging query.
options.D: Create an uptime check against the public endpoint.

explanation.summary: CPU utilisation is already exported for Compute Engine instances, so an alerting policy with a 15-minute duration window on that metric, wired to an email notification channel, meets the requirement with no extra instrumentation.

option_breakdown.A: The Ops Agent collects guest-level metrics and logs from VMs; it is not needed for metrics the platform already reports about a resource.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. CPU utilisation is already exported for Compute Engine instances, so an alerting policy with a 15-minute duration window on that metric, wired to an email notification channel, meets the requirement with no extra instrumentation.
option_breakdown.C: A log-based metric turns matching log entries into a countable metric; it is unnecessary when the value is already an exported metric.
option_breakdown.D: Uptime checks probe an endpoint from Google's global locations; they measure external reachability, not internal resource state.

questions.title: Reserve a static internal IP to match a hardcoded address
questions.summary: Reserving a static internal IP address lets you assign a specific, otherwise-ephemeral address to a new instance so a client hardcoded to that address keeps working unmodified.
questions.question: An application looks for its licensing server at the fixed IP 10.0.3.21. You need to deploy the licensing server on Compute Engine without changing the application's configuration, and the app must be able to reach the server at that address. What should you do?

options.A: Reserve 10.0.3.21 as a static internal IP address, and assign it to the licensing server's instance
options.B: Let Compute Engine assign an ephemeral internal IP, then update DNS to point 10.0.3.21 at whatever address is assigned
options.C: Configure the application to use DHCP so it can discover the licensing server automatically
options.D: Assign 10.0.3.21 as the instance's external IP address instead of an internal one

explanation.summary: A static internal IP reservation lets you pin a specific address from the subnet's range to a new instance at creation time, so the licensing server comes up already answering at exactly the address the unmodified application expects.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This directly satisfies 'no change to the application' by making the infrastructure match the hardcoded address, not the other way around.
option_breakdown.B: DNS cannot make 10.0.3.21 resolve to a different actual IP — 10.0.3.21 is itself an IP literal the application is dialing directly, not a hostname DNS could redirect.
option_breakdown.C: The application is described as looking for a fixed IP, not performing any discovery — changing it to use DHCP would itself be an application configuration change, which is exactly what's prohibited.
option_breakdown.D: 10.0.3.21 is a private RFC 1918 address and cannot be used as a public external IP; assigning it as one is not a valid operation.

questions.title: Investigate post-termination access with Data Access logs
questions.summary: Filtering Data Access audit logs by the departed employee's principal email is how you determine, after the fact, exactly which resources they read once their access should already have been revoked.
questions.question: An employee was terminated, but their Google Cloud access was not removed until two weeks later. You need to determine whether this person accessed any sensitive customer information after their termination date. What should you do?

options.A: Search Data Access audit logs, filtering by the employee's email address as the principal, for the two-week window after termination
options.B: Ask the employee's former manager whether they recall seeing any suspicious activity
options.C: Review only Admin Activity logs, since all access by a former employee would appear there
options.D: Reset every credential in the project and treat that as sufficient, since the investigation window has already closed

explanation.summary: Data Access logs record read and other data-plane operations by principal, so filtering by the former employee's identity across the exposure window produces a precise, evidence-based answer to exactly what they read after termination.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is the authoritative, auditable record for 'did this identity read this data,' scoped to the exact window in question.
option_breakdown.B: A manager's recollection is not an audit trail and cannot reliably confirm or rule out specific data access.
option_breakdown.C: Admin Activity logs record configuration and administrative changes, not routine data reads — the read events this investigation needs live in Data Access logs specifically.
option_breakdown.D: Resetting credentials addresses future risk but answers nothing about what already happened during the exposure window — it is not an investigation.

questions.title: Cloud DNS private zone decouples apps from a changing on-prem IP
questions.summary: A Cloud DNS private managed zone gives applications in the VPC a stable hostname to depend on, so an on-premises database's IP address can change without any application reconfiguration.
questions.question: A VPN tunnel connects your VPC to an on-premises network in a hybrid setup. Multiple Google Cloud applications connect to an on-premises database server, and you want to avoid reconfiguring every application's IP setting whenever the database server's IP changes. What should you do?

options.A: Create a Cloud DNS private managed zone attached to the VPC, and configure applications to use the DNS name instead of the IP
options.B: Hardcode the current IP address into every application, and update all of them manually whenever it changes
options.C: Publish the on-premises database's IP in a public DNS zone accessible from the internet
options.D: Set up a Cloud Load Balancer in front of the on-premises server to abstract its IP

explanation.summary: A private zone resolves a stable hostname to whatever IP is current, visible only within the VPC — applications reference the name once, and only the DNS record needs updating whenever the underlying on-premises IP changes.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. This is exactly the indirection layer needed: one DNS record to update instead of every application's configuration.
option_breakdown.B: Hardcoding IPs and updating every application by hand on every IP change is precisely the maintenance burden the requirement asks to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: A public DNS zone exposes an internal, on-premises hostname and IP information to the public internet — an unnecessary security exposure for what should be purely internal name resolution.
option_breakdown.D: Google Cloud load balancers front Google Cloud backends reachable over the VPC — they are not designed to load-balance in front of a single on-premises server reached over a VPN tunnel for this purpose.

questions.title: Export Cloud SQL for a multi-year audit archive
questions.summary: A scheduled Cloud SQL export to an Archive-class bucket produces a portable, long-lived audit copy, distinct from Cloud SQL's built-in automated backups, which are meant for operational recovery over a much shorter retention window.
questions.question: You run a Cloud SQL for MySQL database and need to retain a month-end copy for three years for audit purposes. What should you do?

options.A: Set up a scheduled export on the first of each month, writing the export file to an Archive-class Cloud Storage bucket
options.B: Rely on Cloud SQL's automated backups and extend their retention setting to three years
options.C: Take a manual on-demand backup once a month and leave it inside Cloud SQL's backup store indefinitely
options.D: Enable point-in-time recovery and treat its transaction-log window as the three-year archive

explanation.summary: Automated backups and PITR logs are operational recovery tools with much shorter effective retention; a scheduled export writes a portable SQL/CSV dump outside the database entirely, which is the mechanism actually meant for long-term, multi-year archival to cheap storage.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A scheduled export produces exactly the durable, long-retained, audit-appropriate monthly snapshot this requirement calls for, at Archive-class's lowest storage cost.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud SQL automated backup retention is bounded well short of three years and is designed for operational restore, not long-term audit archival.
option_breakdown.C: Manual backups still live inside Cloud SQL's own backup system, tied to the instance's lifecycle, and are not intended as a standalone multi-year audit trail.
option_breakdown.D: PITR's transaction log window is measured in days, not years — it is built for recovering from a recent incident, not multi-year compliance retention.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud sql export sql INSTANCE_NAME gs://ARCHIVE_BUCKET/export-$(date +%Y-%m).sql --database=DATABASE_NAME

questions.title: An unused GPU usually means missing GPU libraries in the OS
questions.summary: A GPU only gets used once the matching driver and supporting libraries (e.g. CUDA) are installed inside the guest OS — Google doesn't inject them automatically on every image. OS family, vCPU count, and disk space aren't what determines whether the GPU gets used.
questions.question: You attached a GPU to an instance for ML training, but training is unusually slow and the GPU appears idle. What's the most likely cause?

options.A: The GPU driver/libraries aren't installed in the guest OS
options.B: The OS is based on Ubuntu
options.C: The instance has fewer than eight vCPUs
options.D: There isn't enough persistent disk space

explanation.summary: Without the driver/libraries installed in the OS, workloads silently fall back to the CPU — this is by far the most common cause of an idle attached GPU.

option_breakdown.A: Correct — without the driver/libraries installed in the OS, workloads silently fall back to the CPU.
option_breakdown.B: Ubuntu isn't disqualifying — Ubuntu-based images are commonly used for GPU workloads.
option_breakdown.C: There's no eight-vCPU minimum tied to GPU usage.
option_breakdown.D: Disk space availability doesn't determine whether the GPU gets used by a workload.

questions.title: Signed URL for time-limited object access
questions.summary: Signed URLs grant time-bounded object access to callers with no Google identity.
questions.question: A partner without any Google account must download one object from a private Cloud Storage bucket, and the link must stop working after one hour. What should you do?

options.A: Make the bucket publicly readable and remove the permission after an hour.
options.B: Generate a signed URL for the object with a one-hour expiry.
options.C: Grant allAuthenticatedUsers the Storage Object Viewer role on the bucket.
options.D: Send the partner a service account key file limited to that bucket.

explanation.summary: A signed URL embeds a time-bounded signature, so a caller with no Google identity can fetch exactly one object until the URL expires.

option_breakdown.A: Making the bucket public exposes every object to the internet, and relying on someone to revoke it later is not a time limit.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A signed URL embeds a time-bounded signature, so a caller with no Google identity can fetch exactly one object until the URL expires.
option_breakdown.C: allAuthenticatedUsers means any Google account at all, not your partner specifically, and it does not expire.
option_breakdown.D: Service account keys are long-lived credentials that must never be sent to third parties, and they do not expire.

questions.title: Write-only access for an upload-only service account
questions.summary: storage.objectCreator lets a service account write new objects without reading, overwriting or deleting existing ones — legacy access scopes cannot express that boundary.
questions.question: You need to set up permissions for a set of Compute Engine instances so they can write data into a particular Cloud Storage bucket, and nothing more. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Create a service account with the access scope 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/devstorage.write_only'
options.B: Create a service account with the access scope 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform'
options.C: Create a service account and grant it the IAM role roles/storage.objectCreator on that bucket
options.D: Create a service account and grant it the IAM role roles/storage.objectAdmin on that bucket

explanation.summary: objectCreator lets the instances add new objects to the bucket and nothing else — it cannot read, overwrite, or delete, which matches a write-only ingestion pattern exactly.

option_breakdown.A: Legacy access scopes are a coarse, deprecated authorization layer on top of OAuth — Google's current guidance is to grant IAM roles on the resource instead of relying on scopes.
option_breakdown.B: The cloud-platform scope combined with any IAM role the service account holds project-wide is far broader than 'write to one bucket' and violates least privilege.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. objectCreator is the narrowest predefined role that permits writing new objects, scoped to exactly this one bucket.
option_breakdown.D: objectAdmin adds read, overwrite and delete on every object in the bucket — capabilities this write-only workload does not need.

questions.title: Storage Admin for colleagues managing buckets and objects
questions.summary: roles/storage.admin is the predefined role that covers both bucket lifecycle and object management, one tier above objectAdmin's object-only scope.
questions.question: You are the project owner of a Google Cloud project and want to delegate control to colleagues to manage both buckets and files in Cloud Storage. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. Which IAM role should you grant your colleagues?

options.A: roles/storage.objectCreator
options.B: roles/storage.objectAdmin
options.C: roles/storage.admin
options.D: roles/owner

explanation.summary: objectCreator and objectAdmin only reach into objects inside an existing bucket; managing buckets themselves — creating, deleting, changing their configuration — requires the bucket-level roles/storage.admin.

option_breakdown.A: objectCreator only permits adding new objects and cannot manage buckets or edit existing objects at all.
option_breakdown.B: objectAdmin covers full object CRUD but still has no permission to create, delete or configure buckets themselves.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. storage.admin covers full control of both buckets and the objects inside them, which is exactly 'buckets and files.'
option_breakdown.D: Project Owner grants control of every service in the project, not just Cloud Storage — a much larger blast radius than this task needs.

questions.title: Isolating external vendors in Cloud Storage without over-granting
questions.summary: External vendors dropping files for review belong in a bucket dedicated to them with roles/storage.objectAdmin scoped to that bucket — never Owner, which reaches far beyond object management into bucket deletion and IAM policy changes.
questions.question: You are onboarding several external contractors who each need to drop files into a Cloud Storage bucket for your team's review and approval. You want to isolate each vendor from the others and avoid over-granting access. Which of the following should you avoid doing?

options.A: Creating a separate bucket for each vendor
options.B: Granting each vendor the basic Owner role on their respective bucket
options.C: Granting each vendor roles/storage.objectAdmin scoped to only their own bucket
options.D: Sharing each vendor a direct console link to their own bucket

explanation.summary: The basic Owner role is far broader than object management — it includes deleting the bucket itself and changing its IAM policy, permissions no external, temporary party should ever hold. Least privilege calls for a scoped predefined role instead.

option_breakdown.A: A bucket per vendor is exactly the right isolation boundary — nothing wrong with this.
option_breakdown.B: Correct as the practice to avoid. Owner grants far more than object management, including the ability to delete the bucket and rewrite its IAM policy.
option_breakdown.C: objectAdmin scoped to one bucket is the correctly sized role for a vendor managing the objects they drop, without touching bucket-level administration.
option_breakdown.D: Sharing a console link to a bucket the vendor is already authorized on is harmless — it is a convenience URL, not a permission grant.

questions.title: One signed URL for a client that only ever uploads
questions.summary: A client that only writes to an access-controlled bucket can use Cloud Storage's resumable upload feature to need just one signed URL per upload session, issued up front in a POST request that carries no data itself.
questions.question: Your mobile app uploads photos directly to an access-controlled Cloud Storage bucket. You want callers to authenticate with exactly one signed URL per upload — not a fresh signed URL for every chunk of a large file — while your backend never sees the file bytes. What Cloud Storage capability accomplishes this?

options.A: Object Lifecycle Management with an upload-only transition rule
options.B: Uniform bucket-level access combined with a public allUsers write grant
options.C: Resumable uploads — one signed URL, issued via an initial POST that carries no data, authorizes the entire multi-chunk upload session
options.D: Signed download URLs, reused for the upload by setting the HTTP method to PUT client-side

explanation.summary: The documented pattern is exactly this: the signed URL is generated for the resumable-upload session-start POST, which carries no object bytes, and the session ID it returns authorizes every subsequent chunk PUT without needing additional signing.

option_breakdown.A: Object Lifecycle Management governs class transitions and deletion over time; it has nothing to do with authorizing uploads.
option_breakdown.B: A public allUsers write grant is the opposite of 'access-controlled' and a serious anti-pattern — anyone could overwrite or flood the bucket.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. This is the documented resumable-upload-plus-signed-URL pattern for write-only, single-signature access.
option_breakdown.D: A signed URL is cryptographically bound to the HTTP method it was generated for; a download (GET) signed URL cannot be repurposed for an upload by changing the client-side verb.

questions.title: BigQuery jobUser for a small team that keeps changing
questions.summary: roles/bigquery.jobUser grants the ability to run and manage query jobs without dataset administration rights, and binding it to a group absorbs membership churn without touching IAM.
questions.question: Your Google Cloud project uses BigQuery for data warehousing. Your data science team changes membership frequently and has few members. You need to let members of this team run queries, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.D: Create a Google group in Cloud Identity, add each data scientist's account to the group, and grant the group roles/bigquery.jobUser
options.A: Grant each data scientist roles/bigquery.admin individually as they join the team
options.B: Create a Google group, add the data scientists, and grant the group roles/bigquery.dataOwner
options.C: Share a single project-level API key that every data scientist embeds in their query scripts

explanation.summary: jobUser is the predefined role that lets its holder run and manage query jobs (given read access to the relevant datasets) without dataset-administration rights, and a group means adding or removing a team member never touches an IAM binding.

option_breakdown.D: Correct. This is the minimal role for running queries, and the group indirection is exactly what frequent membership churn calls for.
option_breakdown.A: bigquery.admin grants full control over every dataset and job in the project — far beyond 'run queries,' and individual per-user grants don't scale to a churning roster.
option_breakdown.B: dataOwner grants the ability to modify and delete datasets themselves, which running queries does not require.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery does not authenticate with shared static API keys for this purpose, and a shared secret defeats per-user accountability regardless.

questions.title: Auditor sees query history, not table data
questions.summary: Audit trails live in Cloud Logging; metadata access is separate from data access.
questions.question: An external auditor needs to review your organisation's BigQuery usage. The auditor must be able to see which queries were run, by whom, and against which datasets, but must not be able to read any of the data in the tables or run queries of their own. You want to follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the auditor the BigQuery Data Viewer role on the project.
options.B: Grant the auditor the BigQuery User role on the project.
options.C: Grant the auditor the Logs Viewer role and the BigQuery Metadata Viewer role on the project.
options.D: Grant the auditor the Project Viewer role and export BigQuery data to a bucket they can read.

explanation.summary: Query activity is recorded in Cloud Logging as BigQuery audit logs, so Logs Viewer is what surfaces 'who ran what'. BigQuery Metadata Viewer adds the ability to list datasets, tables and schemas without granting any read access to row data.

option_breakdown.A: BigQuery Data Viewer grants read access to the contents of tables — exactly the data the auditor must not see.
option_breakdown.B: BigQuery User allows the auditor to run their own query jobs and create datasets, exceeding a read-only audit role and incurring cost.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Logs Viewer exposes the audit trail of executed queries and their principals; Metadata Viewer exposes dataset and table structure without row data.
option_breakdown.D: Project Viewer is a broad legacy role, and exporting the data to Cloud Storage hands the auditor the very data you are withholding.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
  --member='user:auditor@example.com' --role='roles/logging.viewer'
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
  --member='user:auditor@example.com' --role='roles/bigquery.metadataViewer'

questions.title: Auditor may view but not modify a project
questions.summary: Because domain restricted sharing blocks external members, the auditor needs an account in your domain granted Viewer on the project.
questions.question: Management has asked an external auditor to review all resources in one project. Domain Restricted Sharing is enabled on the organisation node for your Cloud Identity domain only. The auditor must view, but not modify, the resources in that project. What should you do?

options.A: Grant roles/viewer on the project to the auditor's personal Gmail account.
options.B: Grant roles/editor on the project and ask the auditor not to change anything.
options.C: Create a Cloud Identity account for the auditor in your domain and grant it roles/viewer on the project.
options.D: Disable Domain Restricted Sharing on the organisation for the duration of the audit.

explanation.summary: An account in your domain passes Domain Restricted Sharing, and Viewer grants read-only access to the project's resources.

option_breakdown.A: Domain Restricted Sharing rejects any principal outside your Cloud Identity domain, so the binding cannot be created.
option_breakdown.B: Editor allows modification, which the requirement forbids; trust is not a control.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An account in your domain passes Domain Restricted Sharing, and Viewer grants read-only access to the project's resources.
option_breakdown.D: Relaxing an organisation-wide guardrail for one user weakens it for everyone.

questions.title: Monitor Spanner without touching table data
questions.summary: roles/monitoring.viewer covers dashboards and metrics with zero Spanner data-plane access.
questions.question: You built an application on Google Cloud that uses Cloud Spanner. Your support team needs to monitor the environment but should not have access to table data. You need a streamlined solution to grant the correct permissions to your support team, and you want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.B: Add the support team group to the roles/monitoring.viewer role
options.C: Add the support team group to the roles/spanner.databaseUser role
options.D: Add the support team group to the roles/spanner.databaseReader role
options.A: Grant the support team the Spanner Admin role and restrict it with an IAM condition on business hours

explanation.summary: roles/monitoring.viewer is scoped entirely to Cloud Monitoring's dashboards, metrics and uptime checks — it carries no Spanner permission at all, so it structurally cannot expose table data.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. The support team only needs to observe health and performance signals; monitoring.viewer grants exactly that and nothing in the Spanner API surface.
option_breakdown.C: databaseUser can read and write table rows — the opposite of what 'no access to table data' requires.
option_breakdown.D: databaseReader still grants read access to every row in every table, which violates the stated constraint.
option_breakdown.A: A time-boxed IAM condition still leaves full admin data access during the allowed window; it narrows *when*, not *what*, and Spanner Admin includes data access regardless.

questions.title: Grant Spanner table read-write without the admin surface
questions.summary: roles/spanner.databaseUser is the predefined role for reading and writing table data, and it belongs on a group, not three individual accounts.
questions.question: You need to grant access for three users so that they can view and edit table data on a Cloud Spanner instance, following Google-recommended IAM practices. What should you do?

options.A: Grant each of the three users the Spanner Admin role directly on the instance
options.B: Add the three users to a Google group, and grant that group the roles/spanner.databaseUser role on the database
options.C: Add the three users to a Google group, and grant that group the roles/spanner.databaseReader role on the database
options.D: Give each user a downloaded service account key scoped to roles/spanner.databaseUser

explanation.summary: databaseUser grants read and write on table data without instance- or database-level administration, and binding it once to a group keeps membership changes out of the IAM policy entirely.

option_breakdown.A: Spanner Admin also covers schema changes, backups and instance configuration — far more than 'view and edit table data' requires.
