option_breakdown.B: Correct. databaseUser is exactly read+write on table data, and a group is the maintainable unit for three people who will change over time.
option_breakdown.C: databaseReader is read-only; these users also need to edit data, which this role does not permit.
option_breakdown.D: A human never needs a service account key to authenticate as themselves — that swaps an auditable identity for a long-lived credential for no benefit.

questions.title: Replicate custom IAM roles into a new project
questions.summary: gcloud iam roles copy duplicates a custom role definition into another project or organization in one command, without re-authoring its permission list.
questions.question: You have a development project with appropriate custom IAM roles already defined. You are creating a production project and want the same custom roles available there, using the fewest possible steps. What should you do?

options.A: Manually recreate each custom role in the production project by re-entering its permission list
options.B: Use gcloud iam roles copy, specifying the production project as the destination
options.C: Export the development project's IAM policy and import it into the production project
options.D: Create an organization-level custom role so both projects inherit it automatically

explanation.summary: gcloud iam roles copy reads an existing custom role's title, description, stage and permission list and creates an identical role at the destination project, organization, or even a different resource entirely.

option_breakdown.A: Retyping every permission is exactly the manual, error-prone work the copy command exists to eliminate — not the fewest-steps path.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. One command reproduces the full role definition at the destination with no risk of a transcription mistake.
option_breakdown.C: IAM policies are bindings (who has which role on which resource) — exporting one does not carry the custom role *definitions* themselves.
option_breakdown.D: Moving the role to the organization node changes its scope and visibility for every project underneath it, which is a bigger change than the task calls for and was not requested.

questions.title: External auditor needs logs and BigQuery data in one grant
questions.summary: Audit logging and data access are separate permission surfaces, so a compliant auditor role needs both a logging role and a BigQuery data role.
questions.question: You need to configure IAM access so that an external auditors group can view BigQuery audit logging activity and read the underlying dataset contents. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.B: Add the auditors group to the roles/logging.viewer and roles/bigquery.dataViewer predefined roles
options.C: Add the auditors group to the roles/owner role on the project
options.D: Add the auditors group to the roles/bigquery.admin role only
options.A: Add the auditors group to the roles/logging.viewer role only

explanation.summary: logging.viewer grants read access to the project's logs (including BigQuery's audit trail), while bigquery.dataViewer grants read access to table contents — the two roles together, and only together, cover both halves of the ask.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. This pairing gives exactly log visibility plus data read access, with no write or administrative capability anywhere.
option_breakdown.C: Owner grants full control of every resource in the project, wildly exceeding a read-only audit mandate.
option_breakdown.D: bigquery.admin can create, delete and modify datasets and jobs — the auditor should never be able to change what they are reviewing.
option_breakdown.A: logging.viewer alone shows who ran which query, but grants no permission to read the table data itself.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member=group:auditors@example.com --role=roles/logging.viewer && gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member=group:auditors@example.com --role=roles/bigquery.dataViewer

questions.title: Cross-project service account bound where the resource lives
questions.summary: An IAM binding always lives on the resource being protected, so a service account from one project is authorized by granting it a role in the target resource's own project.
questions.question: You have one project called proj-sa where you manage all your service accounts. You want to use a service account from this project to take snapshots of VMs running in another project called proj-vm. What should you do?

options.B: Grant the service account the IAM role roles/compute.storageAdmin in proj-vm
options.C: Grant the service account the IAM role roles/compute.storageAdmin in proj-sa
options.D: Grant the service account the IAM role roles/owner in proj-sa
options.A: Move the service account into proj-vm before granting it any role

explanation.summary: IAM permission always attaches to the resource's own project — a service account can be identity-homed in proj-sa and still hold a role bound in proj-vm, exactly as a human user could.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. roles/compute.storageAdmin includes snapshot management, and binding it in proj-vm is where the VMs and their disks actually live.
option_breakdown.C: A binding in proj-sa has no effect on resources in proj-vm — the two projects are separate IAM scopes.
option_breakdown.D: Owner in the service account's home project grants nothing on proj-vm's resources and is far broader than snapshot management besides.
option_breakdown.A: Service accounts do not need to be relocated to be granted cross-project permissions — that is the entire point of IAM being resource-scoped, not identity-scoped.

questions.title: Custom role that removes delete as a guardrail
questions.summary: Subtracting the delete permission from a predefined role's baseline into a custom role lets users query freely while making dataset deletion structurally impossible for them.
questions.question: Your organization needs to grant users the ability to query datasets in BigQuery but prevent them from accidentally deleting the datasets. You want a solution that follows Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Grant users the predefined roles/bigquery.dataEditor role
options.B: Create a custom role that starts from the needed BigQuery permissions but omits bigquery.datasets.delete, and grant it to a group containing the users
options.C: Grant users the predefined roles/bigquery.admin role and rely on Cloud Audit Logs to detect accidental deletions
options.D: Grant users roles/bigquery.dataViewer and ask them to request temporary elevation whenever they need to run a query

explanation.summary: A custom role is the only way to grant a permission set that no predefined role expresses — here, query and read access with the single destructive permission removed, so deletion is prevented by IAM rather than by process.

option_breakdown.A: dataEditor includes delete permission on tables and datasets — it does not enforce the constraint the organization actually wants.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Building the role from exactly the needed permissions, minus delete, makes accidental deletion impossible rather than merely discouraged.
option_breakdown.C: Detecting a deletion after it happened does not prevent it — audit logs are for investigation, not guardrails.
option_breakdown.D: dataViewer cannot run queries against data it does not already have read access framed for, and a manual elevation workflow adds friction without actually blocking delete once elevated.

questions.title: Minimum role to just see the folder tree
questions.summary: roles/browser exposes the resource hierarchy's structure with no permission to view or modify anything inside the resources themselves.
questions.question: Your company has hundreds of folders and projects arranged in a complex organizational structure on Google Cloud. Only a few team members should be able to view this hierarchical structure. You want to assign the minimum permissions necessary, following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.A: Add the users to a group, and grant that group roles/viewer at the organization node
options.B: Add the users to a group, and grant that group roles/browser at the organization node
options.C: Add the users to a group, and grant that group roles/resourcemanager.folderAdmin at the organization node
options.D: Add the users individually to roles/owner on each folder they need to see

explanation.summary: roles/browser grants read-only visibility into the names and structure of folders and projects and nothing about the resources living inside them — the narrowest role that satisfies 'see the hierarchy.'

option_breakdown.A: roles/viewer at the org node grants read access to every resource under every project — vastly more than seeing folder and project names.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Browser is purpose-built for exactly this: hierarchy visibility with no resource-level access at all.
option_breakdown.C: folderAdmin allows creating, moving and deleting folders — an administrative capability far beyond simple viewing.
option_breakdown.D: Owner per folder is both broader than needed and does not scale to hundreds of folders — the org-node group binding is the maintainable and minimal approach.

questions.title: One role for whoever creates and manages every service account
questions.summary: roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin covers full service account lifecycle management without granting any other project permission.
questions.question: One person in your organization is responsible for creating and managing all service accounts across your Google Cloud projects. You need to assign this person the minimum role required for each project. What should you do?

options.B: Grant the user roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin on each project
options.C: Grant the user roles/owner on each project
options.D: Grant the user roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on each project
options.A: Grant the user roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin on each project

explanation.summary: serviceAccountAdmin covers creating, deleting, updating and disabling service accounts — the full lifecycle this person needs — and grants nothing about the rest of the project.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. This role is scoped exactly to service account lifecycle management, matching the stated responsibility with no excess.
option_breakdown.C: Owner grants control over every resource in the project, far beyond service account administration alone.
option_breakdown.D: serviceAccountUser lets someone *act as* a service account (attach it to a resource or impersonate it) — it does not permit creating or deleting accounts.
option_breakdown.A: serviceAccountKeyAdmin only manages keys on existing service accounts; it cannot create or delete the accounts themselves, so it does not cover the full stated responsibility.

questions.title: Data Access logs need their own reader role
questions.summary: roles/logging.privateLogViewer is required in addition to a base logging role before Data Access log entries — which carry more sensitive detail than Admin Activity entries — become visible.
questions.question: You need to assign an IAM role to an external auditor. The auditor must be able to review your Cloud Audit Logs, including Data Access logs. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the auditor roles/logging.viewer only
options.B: Grant the auditor roles/logging.privateLogViewer
options.C: Grant the auditor roles/owner so no log category is hidden
options.D: Grant the auditor roles/logging.admin

explanation.summary: Data Access log entries are treated as more sensitive than Admin Activity entries and are gated behind privateLogViewer specifically — logging.viewer alone does not surface them.

option_breakdown.A: logging.viewer shows Admin Activity, System Event, and Policy Denied logs, but Data Access entries stay hidden without the private-log role.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. privateLogViewer is the role built specifically to expose Data Access log entries to a reader.
option_breakdown.C: Owner is unrelated to log visibility specifically and grants enormous unrelated write access across the project — the wrong tool for a read-only audit need.
option_breakdown.D: logging.admin can configure sinks, exclusions and retention — administrative capability the auditor does not need and should not have.

questions.title: Custom role permission stage and support level before go-live
questions.summary: A custom role's permissions must carry the 'supported' support level for production use, and its own launch stage communicates maturity to the rest of the organization.
questions.question: You are creating the first version of a new custom IAM role for use with a Google Cloud service. Every permission in the role must be suitable for production use, and you want to clearly communicate the role's maturity to the rest of your organization while you finish testing it. What should you do?

options.B: Include only permissions with the 'supported' support level, and set the role's launch stage to ALPHA while you finish testing
options.C: Include permissions regardless of support level, and set the launch stage to GA immediately
options.D: Include only permissions with the 'supported' support level, and leave the launch stage unset
options.A: Include only permissions with the 'testing' support level, and set the launch stage to BETA

explanation.summary: Custom roles track two independent signals: each underlying permission carries Google's own support-level guarantee, and the role itself carries a launch stage you set to communicate how far along your own rollout is.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. 'Supported' permissions are the ones Google guarantees are safe to grant in production, and ALPHA truthfully signals the role is still being validated.
option_breakdown.C: Unsupported or testing-only permissions can change or be withdrawn without notice — a poor foundation for anything production-bound — and GA falsely claims the role is finished before testing is done.
option_breakdown.D: Leaving the stage unset hides exactly the maturity signal the requirement asks you to communicate.
option_breakdown.A: 'Testing' support level permissions are explicitly not guaranteed for production use, which directly conflicts with the stated requirement.

questions.title: Application Default Credentials need only the right role on the VM
questions.summary: Application Default Credentials resolve to whatever identity is available in the current environment, so moving from a developer's user login to a Compute Engine VM's attached service account needs no code change — only the right IAM grant on that service account.
questions.question: You built an application on your development laptop that uses Application Default Credentials to call Google Cloud services, and it works there under your own user login. You want to migrate the application to a Compute Engine VM and set up authentication using Google-recommended practices with minimal changes to the code. What should you do?

options.B: Assign the service account attached to the Compute Engine VM the IAM roles the application needs
options.C: Embed your personal user credentials as a downloaded key file and ship it with the application
options.D: Rewrite the application to call gcloud auth login on every startup
options.A: Create a new OAuth client ID and modify the application to complete an interactive consent flow on the VM

explanation.summary: The ADC library checks, in order, an explicit key file, then the gcloud user login, then the metadata server — on a VM the third source kicks in automatically and hands the application short-lived tokens for whatever service account is attached, with zero code change.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. ADC finds the VM's attached service account automatically; the only remaining work is granting that service account the right roles.
option_breakdown.C: Shipping a personal user's credentials as a static file trades a well-scoped, short-lived VM identity for a long-lived, broadly-scoped secret sitting on disk.
option_breakdown.D: gcloud auth login requires interactive browser consent and is not a viable non-interactive server-side authentication path at all.
option_breakdown.A: An interactive OAuth consent flow is built for end-user applications, not for a service running unattended on a VM, and it is a large code change besides.

questions.title: Own-organization SA can't reach a partner's dataset
questions.summary: Sharing a BigQuery dataset across organizations means granting a role to a service account that the partner creates and controls in their own project, not one of yours.
questions.question: You run a data warehouse on BigQuery. A partner company runs a recommendation engine on their own Google Cloud project and needs read access to a dataset in your project. You want to provide access using Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.B: Ask the partner to create a service account in their own project, and grant that service account roles/bigquery.dataViewer on your dataset
options.C: Create a service account in your project, download its key, and email the key file to the partner
options.D: Grant the partner's entire Google Cloud organization roles/bigquery.admin on your project
options.A: Export the dataset to a public Cloud Storage bucket so the partner can download it

explanation.summary: The partner authenticates as an identity they themselves control and audit, while you grant that specific identity exactly dataViewer on exactly the one dataset — no shared secret changes hands and no organization-wide trust is required.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. This keeps the identity under the partner's own control and the grant scoped to a single dataset and role.
option_breakdown.C: A downloaded key emailed across companies is a long-lived, unrotatable secret outside your control the moment it leaves your inbox.
option_breakdown.D: Granting the partner's whole organization admin rights on your project is an enormous, unnecessary blast radius for 'read one dataset.'
option_breakdown.A: A public bucket exposes the data to anyone on the internet, not just the partner, and abandons access control entirely.

questions.title: Authenticate gcloud with a handed-over key file
questions.summary: gcloud auth activate-service-account loads a downloaded JSON key so subsequent gcloud commands run as that service account — the mechanism the workload-identity alternatives exist to avoid.
questions.question: You received a JSON file containing the private key of a service account, granting access to several resources in a Google Cloud project. You have the Cloud SDK installed and want to use this key to authenticate gcloud commands. What should you do?

options.B: Run gcloud auth activate-service-account, pointing it to the private key file
options.C: Paste the contents of the key file into the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable directly as text
options.D: Run gcloud auth login and enter the key file's contents as your password
options.A: Import the key into a new user account in Cloud Identity

explanation.summary: activate-service-account is the command purpose-built to authenticate the gcloud CLI as a service account from a downloaded key, after which every subsequent command runs under that identity until you switch accounts.

option_breakdown.B: Correct. This is the documented, direct way to authenticate gcloud itself with a service account key.
option_breakdown.C: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS expects a *path* to the key file for ADC-consuming client libraries, not the file's contents, and it does not authenticate the gcloud CLI's own commands.
option_breakdown.D: gcloud auth login is the interactive human-login flow; it does not accept a service account key as a substitute for a password.
option_breakdown.A: A service account is not a human user and cannot be 'imported' as one — mixing the two identity types this way is not a supported operation.

questions.title: Audit who holds Project Owner from the command line
questions.summary: gcloud projects get-iam-policy prints the project's full IAM policy, letting you filter directly for every principal bound to the Owner role during a security review.
questions.question: A colleague handed you a Google Cloud project to maintain. As part of a security checkup, you want to review exactly who has been granted the Project Owner role. What should you do?

options.C: Run gcloud projects get-iam-policy to view the current role bindings
options.D: Ask every team member individually whether they believe they have Owner access
options.A: Assume nobody has Owner unless you personally granted it, since Owner is not inherited from anywhere
options.B: Delete and recreate the project so you start with a clean IAM policy

explanation.summary: The IAM policy is the authoritative source of every role binding on the project; printing it (optionally filtered to roles/owner) gives a complete, accurate list with no reliance on anyone's memory or assumptions.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. This directly and completely answers 'who has Owner' from the source of truth, in one command.
option_breakdown.D: Self-reported access is unreliable — people forget grants, and inherited bindings from a folder or organization node wouldn't show up in anyone's personal assumption either.
option_breakdown.A: Owner absolutely can be inherited from a folder or organization-level binding, so assuming otherwise risks missing exactly the access this review is meant to find.
option_breakdown.B: Recreating the project is drastic, destroys every existing resource, and does nothing to answer who currently has access — it also isn't a security review at all.

questions.title: A custom role that predefined-role updates can't silently widen
questions.summary: Because Google can add new permissions to a predefined role over time, a team bound to that role can gain access nobody explicitly granted — a custom role is immune to that drift since only you control what it contains.
questions.question: Your DevOps team needs access to a large number of production Google Cloud services concentrated in a single project. You want to prevent future Google Cloud product changes from silently broadening the team's permissions. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.C: Create a custom role that combines exactly the required permissions, and grant it to the DevOps team on the production project
options.D: Grant the DevOps team the closest matching predefined roles, and review the permission list manually every quarter
options.A: Grant the DevOps team roles/editor, since it already covers most of the services they need
options.B: Grant the DevOps team roles/viewer, and separately request elevated access whenever a specific task requires it

explanation.summary: Predefined roles are maintained by Google and can gain new permissions as products evolve, silently expanding what anyone holding that role can do — a custom role's permission list only changes when you change it, which is exactly the guarantee 'prevent future changes from broadening permissions' calls for.

option_breakdown.C: Correct. A custom role is the only option whose permission set cannot drift wider without your own explicit action, directly satisfying the stated goal.
option_breakdown.D: A quarterly manual review is a detective control that catches drift after it has already occurred — it does not prevent the permissions from having silently broadened in the meantime.
option_breakdown.A: Editor is both far broader than the team's actual production needs today and just as subject to future permission growth as any other predefined role.
option_breakdown.B: Viewer plus ad hoc elevation requests is an operational burden for routine work, and says nothing about preventing predefined-role drift for whatever role each elevation request ends up granting.

questions.title: Compute Storage Admin is the role for managing snapshots
questions.summary: Compute Storage Admin (roles/compute.storageAdmin) grants full control over Compute Engine's storage resources — disks, images, and snapshots — which is exactly the scope needed to delegate backup-snapshot creation without granting broader project access.
questions.question: You want to delegate the ability to create backup snapshots to one team member, without granting broader project access. Which predefined role should you grant?

options.A: Compute Image Admin
options.B: Storage Admin
options.C: Compute Snapshot Admin
options.D: Compute Storage Admin

explanation.summary: Compute Storage Admin covers Compute Engine disks, images, and snapshots — exactly the scope needed here. The other role names either don't exist or target the wrong resource type.

option_breakdown.A: 'Compute Image Admin' isn't a real predefined Compute Engine role.
option_breakdown.B: Storage Admin (roles/storage.admin) controls Cloud Storage buckets/objects — an entirely different service from Compute Engine snapshots.
option_breakdown.C: 'Compute Snapshot Admin' isn't a real predefined role name.
option_breakdown.D: Correct — Compute Storage Admin is the real predefined role covering Compute Engine disks, images, and snapshots.

questions.title: Changing the service account of a running VM
questions.summary: A VM's service account and access scopes can only be changed while the VM is stopped.
questions.question: A VM runs as the default compute service account. You created a dedicated least-privilege service account and want the VM to use it. What must you do?

options.A: Run gcloud compute instances set-service-account on the running VM.
options.B: Delete and recreate the VM; the service account cannot be changed.
options.C: Grant the new service account roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on the old one.
options.D: Stop the VM, set the new service account (and scopes) on it, then start it.

explanation.summary: A VM's attached service account can be changed, but only while the instance is stopped.

option_breakdown.A: The command exists but fails on a running instance.
option_breakdown.B: Recreating is unnecessary.
option_breakdown.C: That lets one account act as the other; it does not change what the VM runs as.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A VM's attached service account can be changed, but only while the instance is stopped.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop app-1 --zone=us-central1-a
gcloud compute instances set-service-account app-1 --zone=us-central1-a \
  --service-account=app-sa@P.iam.gserviceaccount.com --scopes=cloud-platform
gcloud compute instances start app-1 --zone=us-central1-a
